summary: John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster (1340-1399), was the third surviving son of Edward III and the patriarch of the Lancastrian dynasty — father of Henry IV, grandfather of Henry V, great-grandfather of the Henry VI now on the throne. anchor_text: Thy grandfather, Roger Mortimer, Earl of March
summary: Henry is rehearsing York's genealogy to undercut his claim. York's grandfather was Roger Mortimer, 4th Earl of March (d. 1398), and through Roger's mother Philippa of Clarence — daughter of Edward III's second surviving son, Lionel — the Mortimer line ran senior to the Lancastrian descent from John of Gaunt (the third son). Henry mentions Roger Mortimer not to concede the point but to re-frame York as a subject line, not a royal one.

anchor_text: Talk not of France, sith thou hast lost it all

Henry V's treaty of Troyes (1420) had made him heir to the French throne; under Henry VI, all the English territories were systematically lost by 1453, with only Calais remaining. Warwick weaponizes this failure: invoking Henry V's glory only highlights Henry VI's failure.

anchor_text: Henry the Fourth by conquest got the crown. 'T was by rebellion against his king
summary: Henry VI is forced to argue that his great-grandfather Bolingbroke (Henry IV) won the crown by conquest — then in the same breath admits privately that the conquest was rebellion. This is the Lancastrian title's fatal flaw: Henry IV deposed the anointed Richard II by force, so the Lancastrian line was built on a defect from the start. Henry VI knows this, and the aside that follows ('I know not what to say; my title's weak') shows he cannot answer York's counter-argument.
detail: The exchange crystallizes the constitutional crisis of the whole first tetralogy. Henry IV's usurpation of 1399 (dramatized in Richard II) is the original wound; every Lancastrian king since has governed under a cloud of questionable title. Holinshed and Hall both discuss at length whether conquest, parliamentary sanction, or lineal right determines the crown — and the plays exploit that ambiguity throughout.

anchor_text: May that ground gape and swallow me alive, Where I shall kneel to him that slew my father

Clifford himself will never kneel to York — he helps kill him — so by his own logic the oath is fulfilled.

anchor_text: I here entail The crown to thee, and to thine heirs for ever
summary: To 'entail' property or a title means to settle it on a specified line of heirs so that it cannot be sold, given away, or diverted — the legal device prevents future owners from breaking the chain of inheritance. Henry is using precise legal language: by entailing the crown to York and his heirs, he is not merely promising it, he is making a formal disposition that treats the crown as property to be settled.
detail: The irony is sharp: Henry is using a device designed to protect inheritance against disruption to disinherit his own son. The Act of Accord of 1460 — the historical document Shakespeare is dramatizing — did exactly this: it confirmed Henry as king for life but barred his son Prince Edward from the succession and settled the crown on York's line. The Lancastrian lords storm out because they understand the full legal weight of 'entail.'

Exeter's pious imprecation ('Accurs'd be he that seeks to make them foes') is answered within fifty lines by the woman who will make them foes again. It also echoes the formal curse that ends oaths of peace throughout the play, many of which are quickly broken.

anchor_text: what is it but to make thy sepulchre And creep into it far before thy time
summary: Margaret uses a vivid metaphor: by entailing the crown to York, Henry has dug his own grave and is now crawling into it ahead of schedule. summary: Margaret uses an animal fable image — a lamb surrounded by wolves — to measure how much 'safety' Henry's agreement actually provides. The word 'environed' means encircled or surrounded. anchor_text: I here divorce myself, Both from thy table, Henry, and thy bed
summary: Margaret does not mean a legal divorce but a formal separation: she withdraws from sharing Henry's table (meals, household) and bed (marital relations) until the Act of Parliament disinheriting her son is repealed. The formula 'table and bed' echoes the language of medieval and canon law on marital rights — a wife's basic entitlements were food, clothing, and conjugal rights. By withdrawing from both, Margaret is signalling that she no longer recognises Henry as a functioning husband or king.
detail: The public declaration is also a political statement: Margaret is announcing that she, not Henry, will lead the Lancastrian cause. In canon law a wife could separate from a husband 'from bed and board' (a mensa et thoro) on grounds of cruelty without dissolving the marriage itself. Margaret inverts this: Henry has done nothing cruel to her, but he has done something unforgivable to their son. The theatricality is deliberate — she is announcing a political divorce of leadership, not just a domestic separation.

anchor_text: haughty spirit, winged with desire, Will cost my crown, and like an empty eagle Tire on the flesh of me and of my son
summary: 'Haughty' meant high-spirited or proud (from French 'haut,' high — not yet as negative as it sounds today). 'Tire' is falconry language: a hawk 'tires on' its prey when it tears at the flesh with its beak. An 'empty' eagle is a hungry one (from French 'vide'). Henry pictures York as a famished eagle that will devour both Henry and his son once it has the crown. The image inverts the earlier falconry metaphor Warwick used proudly — here the bird of prey is a threat, not a symbol of power.
detail: The eagle was the traditional emblem of royal power and the noblest of birds in the bestiary tradition, so calling York an eagle who will 'tire' on the king's flesh is itself a de casibus image: the legitimate king is prey to the beast that should be his symbol. Shakespeare returns to this predatory-eagle image throughout the play.

anchor_text: for a kingdom any oath may be broken
summary: Edward argues that an oath taken to a king can be broken when a crown is at stake. Elizabethan orthodoxy held the opposite: an oath sworn on the Gospels was a sacred bond enforced by God, and perjury was a mortal sin. Edward's breezy exception — 'I would break a thousand oaths to reign one year' — signals the Yorkist faction's ruthlessness from the outset.
detail: The tension between political necessity and the sanctity of oaths is a recurring engine of the history plays. York swore at the Parliament in Act 1 Scene 1 to let Henry reign for life in exchange for the succession; his son's willingness to smash that oath in the same breath exposes the Yorkist compact as expedient rather than principled. Holinshed records York's agreement but passes quickly over its breach, leaving Shakespeare to give it this pointed, dramatic scrutiny. The scene anticipates Richard III's much colder version of the same logic: oaths are instruments to be deployed and discarded.

The reading that Edward's breezy oath-breaking signals Yorkist expediency is textually grounded (TLN 295 makes it explicit) and the connection to York's Act of Accord oath from 1.1 is a mainstream dramatic irony the scene directly sets up.

anchor_text: An oath is of no moment, being not took / Before a true and lawful magistrate
summary: Richard (the future Richard III) argues that an oath sworn before an unlawful authority has no legal force, since the swearer owed no obedience to the one who administered it. His reasoning: Henry VI is a usurper, not a 'true and lawful magistrate,' so any oath sworn to him is null. This precocious legal sophistry, constructed on the spot to free his father from a scruple, signals the cold, casuistical intellect that will define Richard's career.
detail: The argument draws on a real strand of late-medieval canon law: oaths sworn under duress or before an incompetent authority could be annulled. But Richard applies the logic aggressively and self-servingly — he is using a legitimate doctrinal distinction to rationalize political convenience. The speech is one of the earliest glimpses of the future Richard III as an operator who weaponizes law and reason. The underlying Yorkist position (Henry's title is defective because it descends from Bolingbroke's usurpation of the anointed Richard II) is the same genealogical argument that the York family has pressed since Henry IV; Richard here gives it a fresh, casuistical twist. Compare Richard's own later soliloquy (3.2) where he explicitly boasts of the same capacity for persuasion and deception.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Yorkist claim and the Parliament of 1460.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 300

Holinshed 1587 on the Yorkist genealogical claim and the Parliament of 1460 is a real, relevant source; Schmidt s.v. 'moment' meaning weight or importance is a standard Shakespearean sense well within Schmidt's documented lexicon.

Richard's casuistical argument that an oath before an unlawful authority is void draws on a genuine strand of canon law, and reading this speech as an early signal of his manipulative intelligence is a mainstream scholarly position, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: Within whose circuit is Elysium / And all that poets feign of bliss and joy
summary: Elysium (also called the Elysian Fields) was the paradise of classical myth where the souls of heroes and the virtuous dwelt after death in perpetual happiness. Richard uses it as shorthand for perfect, imagined bliss. 'That poets feign' acknowledges this is poetic legend, not literal fact — but the rhetorical point is that wearing a crown is as good as paradise.
detail: Virgil describes Elysium in Aeneid 6.637-678: wide green meadows, a brighter sun, games, music, feasting, and the souls of those who deserved well of their country. Ovid and other classical poets repeated the image. By Shakespeare's day Elysium was a common poetic shorthand for heaven-on-earth happiness. Richard's choice of a pagan rather than a Christian paradise is characteristic of his secular, calculating temperament; it also signals that his vision of the crown is sensual and worldly rather than spiritual. The phrase 'poets feign' (meaning 'poets invent or imagine') was standard Elizabethan acknowledgment that classical mythology was fiction, not Scripture.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.637-678 (the Elysian Fields; the blessed dead in paradise).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'feign' (to invent, imagine, as of poetic fiction).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 308

Virgil Aeneid 6.637-678 is confirmed as the Elysian Fields section (games, music, blessed heroes); Onions s.v. 'feign' is confirmed and explicitly cites this very line (3H6 1.2.31) as its illustrative example.

The Elysium allusion and Aeneid 6 citation are sound, but the interpretive inference that Richard's choice of a pagan rather than Christian paradise reveals his 'secular, calculating temperament' overreaches — use of classical myth as rhetorical shorthand for bliss was a standard Elizabethan poetic convention requiring no special secular disposition.

anchor_text: the white rose that I wear be dyed / Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry's heart
summary: The white rose was the badge of the house of York; the red rose was the badge of the house of Lancaster. Richard says he will not rest until his white rose is stained red with the blood of King Henry VI. The image collapses the play's central symbolic opposition — white rose versus red — into a single, violent act of transformation. It also foreshadows the future: Richard will eventually murder Henry VI in the Tower (5.6).
detail: The rose badges were genuine heraldic emblems: the white rose a Yorkist device, the red rose associated with Lancaster. Shakespeare dramatized the adoption of these symbols in 1 Henry VI 2.4 (the Temple Garden scene), where nobles pluck red or white roses to declare their allegiance. That scene was probably written after this play, but it served as a retrospective origin myth for a conflict that hardened over decades. The detail of 'lukewarm blood' (blood that has just left the living body) adds a physiological specificity that makes the image brutal rather than merely rhetorical. Richard's willingness to voice this bloodlust in his father's presence — going beyond even Edward's impatience — marks him as the most ferocious of the York brothers.

sources.name: Edward Hall, Union (1548)
sources.citation: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548), on the Yorkist white-rose badge and the Lancastrian red rose.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 311

Hall's Union (1548) is a real and relevant source that covers the Yorkist white-rose badge and the Lancastrian red rose; the citation is legitimate even though modern scholarship notes the red-rose Lancastrian badge was not consistently used during the actual conflict.

The Yorkist white-rose badge, its contrast with the Lancastrian red rose, and the foreshadowing of Richard's murder of Henry VI in 5.6 are all accurate; the note on 1 Henry VI's Temple Garden scene as a later retrospective myth is defensible Shakespeare scholarship.

anchor_text: whet on Warwick to this enterprise
summary: 'Whet' means to sharpen, as one sharpens a blade on a whetstone; figuratively, to urge or incite someone to action. York is sending Montague to sharpen Warwick's appetite for the military enterprise of seizing the crown by force. The metallic metaphor suits the military context: Warwick, the most powerful nobleman in England, needs to be honed to a fighting edge.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 315

The figurative meaning of 'whet' as 'to incite or sharpen' is well-attested in Onions and OED, and the metallic/military metaphor reading is wholly appropriate to context.

anchor_text: A woman-general! what should we fear?
summary: Richard dismisses Queen Margaret as no threat because she is a woman commanding an army — a contempt the play will punish immediately. The Elizabethan assumption that women could not lead armies in the field makes his scorn socially legible, but the play has already shown Margaret to be a ferocious military leader; she will capture York before the next scene ends and execute him herself. For Shakespeare's audience, aware of Queen Elizabeth I's famous Tilbury speech (1588) rallying troops against the Armada, the taunt carried an additional irony.
detail: Margaret's military command was historically real: she raised the northern Lancastrian army and led it to Wakefield, where York was killed, and later to Towton. Holinshed records her energy and strategic direction of the Lancastrian cause across several campaigns. The play repeatedly codes her masculine aggression as unnatural — York calls her 'She-wolf of France' and 'tiger's heart wrapp'd in a woman's hide' (1.4) — while simultaneously staging her effectiveness. Richard's dismissal here is straightforwardly ironic: five men against twenty is a bad bet regardless of the general's sex, and York's army is about to be routed. The line also contrasts with the earlier scene (1.1) where even Westmoreland and Northumberland respect Margaret's power.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Queen Margaret's military campaigns including the Battle of Wakefield, December 1460.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 347

Holinshed covers Margaret's military campaigns broadly, but the source citation specifically claims she 'led' the army to Wakefield (December 1460); historically she was in Scotland at the time, and even Holinshed following Hall attributes battlefield command to the northern earls rather than to Margaret directly at Wakefield — the citation stretches the source.

The dramatic irony of Richard's dismissal against Margaret's demonstrated military effectiveness is textually grounded and the Tilbury allusion is a reasonable authorial-audience resonance for a play written in the early 1590s, though it is an inference rather than a certainty.

anchor_text: Many a battle have I won in France / Whenas the enemy hath been ten to one
summary: 'Whenas' means 'when' or 'at a time when' — an archaic conjunction. York's boast about France recalls the English victories of the Hundred Years' War, particularly the campaigns under Henry V and the early reign of Henry VI, in which York himself served as Regent of France (1436-37 and 1440-45). The memory of those campaigns against the French is York's basis for confidence against an English queen's army — a confidence the play immediately undercuts when the battle goes against him.
detail: Richard, Duke of York held the Regency of France twice during Henry VI's reign and fought in the later campaigns of the Hundred Years' War, the same conflict dramatized in 1 Henry VI. He is invoking genuine military experience, not merely bragging. The comparison of five to twenty against his past ten-to-one odds is meant to show his army's odds as relatively tame by his own standard. The irony the audience would have felt is that in France York was part of a losing cause — by the 1450s the English had been driven out of almost all their French possessions. So the campaigns he cites as proofs of courage were also, in the longer view, campaigns of defeat.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on York's Lieutenancy and Regency of France, c. 1436-45.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'whenas' (conjunction: when, at the time that).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 352

Holinshed does cover York's French appointments (1436-37 and 1440-45) and the dates are accurate, but the citation and annotation prose call his role a 'Regency' when York held the title 'Lieutenant-general and governor,' never formally Regent — this mischaracterises his office as recorded in the historical sources.
York's historical service as Regent of France, the 'whenas' gloss, and the ironic point that his French campaigns were ultimately a losing cause are all accurate and textually relevant.

anchor_text: pent-up lion o'er the wretch / That trembles under his devouring paws
summary: Rutland compares Clifford to a lion that has cornered its prey and toys with it before the kill. 'Pent-up' means cooped or caged — pent energy ready to explode. The four-line simile ('So looks... And so he walks... And so he comes') builds by anaphora (the repeated 'And so he') to slow the approach of death, making the audience feel the same helpless waiting Rutland feels.
detail: Anaphora — the repetition of a phrase at the start of successive clauses — was a standard rhetorical intensifier taught in Elizabethan grammar schools under the Latin name 'anaphora' or 'epanaphora.' Here it also mimics the lion's measured stalking: each new clause is another step nearer. The comparison of a powerful enemy to a lion caging its prey appears in Virgil's Aeneid (e.g., Book 9) and was a commonplace of epic and tragic verse; Tudor schoolboys would have recognized it as a heroic simile turned to ironic, pathetic use — the 'prey' is a child.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pent' adj.: 'confined, shut up, cooped.' First recorded use of 'pent-up' in the figurative sense of suppressed force.

sources.name: Puttenham, Art of English Poesy
sources.citation: George Puttenham, The Arte of English Poesie (1589), Book III, ch. 19: 'Anaphora, or the Figure of Report' — repetition of the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 366

OED s.v. 'pent' is real and supportive; Puttenham does cover anaphora under 'Figure of Report' in Book III, but chapter 19 specifically could not be positively confirmed from available sources — the source and claim are plausible but the chapter number is unverified.

'Pent-up' as confined/suppressed force is accurate, the anaphora ('And so he... And so he') is plainly present in the text, and the epic lion-simile as a heroic figure turned to pathetic/ironic use is a defensible mainstream reading of the passage.

anchor_text: my father's blood / Hath stopp'd the passage where thy words should enter
summary: Clifford tells Rutland that his father York killed Clifford's father at St Albans, and that grief has blocked his ears to any plea. The image is literal-metaphorical: he imagines his dead father's blood as a physical substance plugging the channel through which words reach the heart, making mercy anatomically impossible.
detail: The conceit draws on the early-modern understanding of the ear as a passage to the soul — a channel through which speech could move the affections. By claiming it is filled with blood, Clifford insists that grief has made him a different kind of creature, one no longer reachable by language or pity. Rutland's immediate counter-argument ('Then let my father's blood open it again,' TLN 377) accepts the metaphor and tries to turn it: if the blockage is made of blood, more York blood should dissolve it. The exchange is a compressed rhetorical debate (stichomythia — line-for-line riposte) that gives the scene its horrible irony, as a child tries to argue his way out of death. Holinshed records Clifford's vow of revenge for his father's death at St Albans as the motivation for the killing.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587): the elder Lord Clifford was slain at St Albans (1455) and his son swore revenge on the house of York.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'passage': 'the channel or way through which anything passes, including speech reaching the mind or heart.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 375

Holinshed (1587) does record the elder Clifford's death at St Albans (1455) and his son's sworn revenge on York, and Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real, appropriate lexicographical source for the figurative sense of 'passage'.

The ear-as-passage-to-the-soul conceit is consistent with early-modern faculty psychology, the stichomythic riposte structure (Rutland at TLN 377 immediately mirrors the blood-metaphor) is textually confirmed, and Holinshed's record of Young Clifford's revenge-vow is accurate historical context — no overreach.

anchor_text: sight of any of the house of York / Is as a fury to torment my soul
summary: Clifford compares the sight of any Yorkist to a Fury tormenting his soul. The Furies (Greek Erinyes) were three terrifying goddesses of vengeance in classical myth — Alecto, Megaera, and Tisiphone — who pursued murderers and oath-breakers and drove them mad. To be tormented by a Fury was the classical image for guilt-haunted, unappeasable rage.
detail: In Greek religion the Furies punished crimes against blood-kin above all; their victims, like Orestes after he killed his mother Clytemnestra, were driven to madness by their hounding. The term passed into Latin as Furiae and was familiar to Elizabethans through Virgil (Aeneid 6, where Aeneas sees them in the underworld), Seneca's revenge tragedies (hugely influential on the Elizabethan stage), and Ovid. Clifford's use of the image is grimly ironic: the Furies traditionally punished murderers, but he casts himself as a Fury's victim driven to become a murderer. Holinshed records Young Clifford's ferocity after his father's death at St Albans, attributing it to just such a passion of grief and revenge.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.570-572 (the Furies and their torments in the underworld); Aeneid 12.845-854 (a Fury loosed to drive warriors to madness).

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Young Clifford's vow of merciless revenge after St Albans, continued in the 3 Henry VI narrative.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 384

Aeneid 6 (around lines 555-580) places Tisiphone and the Furies as tormentors in Tartarus, and Aeneid 12.843-868 has Jupiter dispatching a Dira (Fury) to drive warriors; both citations are real and directly support the claim.

Clifford's 'fury' is glossed as the classical Erinyes/Furiae, which is the standard Elizabethan referent for the word in a revenge context; the note that Clifford casts himself as victim rather than agent of vengeance is an accurate and defensible ironic reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: for his sake pity me, / Lest in revenge thereof, sith God is just, / He be as miserably slain as I
summary: 'Sith' is an archaic conjunction meaning 'since' or 'seeing that.' Rutland is telling Clifford: spare me for your own son's sake, since God is just and will repay wrong for wrong — if you kill me, your son may be killed in revenge in turn. The appeal blends practical self-interest (Clifford has a child to lose) with the biblical principle that God returns measure for measure.
detail: The reasoning draws on the lex talionis — the law of equivalent retaliation — embedded in Scripture: 'an eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24; Geneva 1599) and, more pointedly, the warning in Matthew 7:2 'with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.' Rutland's argument is a child's version of the play's whole mechanism: every killing breeds a counter-killing in kind. The irony is terrible — Clifford's son does not appear in the play, but the audience, watching a cycle of revenge already four plays long, knows that the logic Rutland invokes is exactly correct: the Yorkists will in time annihilate the Clifford line. 'Sith' (from Old English 'siththan') was common in the sixteenth century but had passed out of general use by Shakespeare's time; he retains it for its archaic-dignified flavor in verse.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sith' conj.: 'since, seeing that, because.' Archaic by the late 16th century; used for poetic elevation.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 7:2 (Geneva 1599): 'with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again'; cf. Exodus 21:24 on equivalent retaliation.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 395

OED s.v. 'sith' is real and accurate; Geneva Bible 1599 Matthew 7:2 wording ('with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again') matches the quotation, and Exodus 21:24 is the standard lex talionis verse.

'Sith' as archaic 'since/seeing that' is correct; the gloss on the lex talionis logic (Rutland warns Clifford that God's justice will repay the killing in kind through Clifford's own son) is precisely what the lines say and is a mainstream reading, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Dii faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae
summary: Rutland dies cursing Clifford in Latin: 'May the gods grant that this [deed] be the crowning glory of your praise' — that is, may your murder of a helpless child be the finest thing anyone will ever say about you. It is a devastating ironic prayer: the gods are called on to make the killing of a child Clifford's greatest achievement, and so his eternal shame.
detail: The line is drawn from Ovid's Heroides 2.66 (Phyllis to Demophoon) — a letter from a woman abandoned by her lover — where the original curse is 'may this be the pinnacle of your fame.' By putting a classical tag on the dying lips of a boy, Shakespeare signals his education (he is accompanied by a tutor-chaplain) and sharpens the pathos: he is old enough to read Ovid but too young to defend himself. The use of Latin also distances the curse from ordinary English speech, giving it a formal, almost ritual weight — as if Rutland is pronouncing a binding classical imprecation rather than merely screaming. Elizabethan grammar-school boys translated passages of the Heroides; the audience's educated members would catch the allusion and feel the irony the more acutely. Holinshed records Rutland's murder at Wakefield but gives him no last words; the Latin line is Shakespeare's addition.

sources.name: Ovid, Heroides
sources.citation: Ovid, Heroides 2.66 (Phyllis to Demophoon): 'Di faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae' — 'may the gods grant this be the highest pinnacle of your praise.' The line is a sarcastic curse wishing infamy on the addressee.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the murder of the Earl of Rutland at Wakefield after the Battle of Wakefield (December 1460) by Lord Clifford — noted briefly without last words.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 403

The Latin Library text of Heroides 2 confirms 'di faciant, laudis summa sit ista tuae' is at line 66, attributed to Phyllis writing to Demophoon, and the gloss as an ironic curse is accurate; Holinshed's brief record of Rutland's murder at Wakefield is confirmed.

The Ovid Heroides 2.66 source and the ironic-curse reading ('may this be the pinnacle of your praise' = your eternal shame) are accurate; the claim that the Latin signals Rutland's grammar-school education and sharpens the pathos is a sound mainstream reading, and noting that Holinshed gives no last words confirms the line is Shakespeare's addition.

anchor_text: army of the queen hath got the field
summary: The scene is set immediately after the Lancastrian victory at Wakefield (December 1460), where Margaret's army defeated and killed the Duke of York. 'Got the field' means won the battle — 'field' was the standard Elizabethan term for a pitched battle or its site.
detail: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587) records the Battle of Wakefield (30 December 1460) as a Lancastrian ambush in which York was outnumbered and his uncles killed. The 'uncles' York mentions at TLN 409 are Sir John Mortimer and Sir Hugh Mortimer, who died rescuing him. The scene opens mid-flight, with York already knowing the battle is lost — a late entry giving the audience the outcome immediately through a soldier's desperate monologue.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the Battle of Wakefield, 30 December 1460.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 408
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record the Battle of Wakefield (30 December 1460) as a Lancastrian victory in which York was killed; the citation is real and supportive.

'Got the field' as standard Elizabethan idiom for winning a pitched battle is uncontroversial, and the historical frame (Wakefield, December 1460, York's uncles dying in the rescue) matches both Holinshed and the text at TLN 409.

anchor_text: fly like ships before the wind, Or lambs pursu'd by hunger-starved wolves
summary: York uses two rapid similes for his fleeing troops — ships running helplessly before a gale, then lambs chased by starving wolves. The pairing of the helpless and the predatory sharpens the sense of panic before York steadies himself into defiance.
detail: The double simile is characteristic of Shakespeare's formal rhetoric in the history plays: two images from distinct realms (sea and field) that reinforce a single idea. 'Hunger-starved' is an intensive compound, common in Elizabethan usage — 'hunger-starved' meaning famished to the point of frenzy. The contrast between these images of flight and the soldierly resolve York displays moments later ('I am your butt, and I abide your shot') is the scene's first emotional pivot.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 411
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1886) is a real standard reference that documents 'hunger-starved' as an intensive Elizabethan compound; the citation is legitimate and supports the lexical claim.

The double simile (ships before wind, lambs before wolves) is plainly present in the text and the reading of it as paired images of helplessness is mainstream; 'hunger-starved' as an intensive compound is defensible Elizabethan usage.

anchor_text: purple falchion painted to the hilt In blood
summary: A 'falchion' is a curved, broad-bladed sword with a single cutting edge — heavier and less pointed than a rapier. 'Purple' here means dark reddish-crimson, the color of blood drying on metal. York is picturing his son Edward's sword stained with blood to the very guard.
detail: In Elizabethan English 'purple' frequently meant blood-red or crimson rather than the modern blue-purple hue; it was a color associated with royalty and with shed blood alike, a double association Shakespeare exploits throughout the histories. 'Falchion' (from Old French fauchon, from faux, a scythe) was the standard term for a heavy curved sword; Onions notes it could be used loosely for any large sword.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'falchion' and 'purple.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 419
Onions's Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986) is a real reference that covers both 'falchion' (curved sword) and 'purple' (blood-red); the citation accurately supports the claims made.
'Falchion' as a curved heavy sword and 'purple' as blood-crimson (not the modern blue-purple hue) are both well-attested Elizabethan usages, and the text's imagery supports the gloss exactly.

anchor_text: budg'd again, as I have seen a swan With bootless labour swim against the tide
summary: 'Budged' means gave ground or flinched — to 'budge' is to move slightly under pressure, a word used with contempt for retreat. York's simile of a swan exhausting itself fighting a tidal current captures both the beauty and futility of the Yorkist stand: powerful, effortful, and ultimately washed back.
detail: The swan simile is carefully chosen. Swans were associated with nobility and with royal heraldry in England; to liken York's army to a swan laboring against the tide rather than to a common waterfowl flatters the Yorkist cause even in defeat. 'Bootless' means without profit or result (from 'boot,' meaning benefit or advantage, not the footwear) — a common Elizabethan word surviving only in 'bootless errand.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'budge' and 'bootless.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 426
Onions's Shakespeare Glossary covers 'budge' (to give ground) and 'bootless' (unprofitable, from 'boot' meaning benefit); the citation is real and supportive.

'Budge' as flinch/give ground, 'bootless' as profitless (from 'boot' = benefit), and the swan-against-tide simile are all accurately glossed; the association of swans with nobility is a reasonable contextual enrichment without overreaching.

anchor_text: The sands are number'd that make up my life
summary: York figures his remaining moments as grains of sand — finite and countable, almost run out. The image of sand as a measure of time comes from the hourglass, which Elizabethan audiences would have recognized immediately. York is saying he has counted down to his last few moments of life.
detail: The hourglass was the standard Elizabethan emblem of measured, finite time — common in emblems and on memorial engravings of the period. The compressed syntax ('sands... that make up my life') is typical of the histories' urgent style. The line also anticipates the scene's theatrical game: York knows he will die here, and the audience watches him choose how to face it.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1886), s.v. 'sand' (time measured by the glass) and 'number' (to count, reckon up).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 432
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon covers 'sand' in the sense of time measured by an hourglass and 'number' as to count or reckon; the citation is real and supports the hourglass-time reading.

The hourglass as the standard Elizabethan emblem of finite time is solid, and the line's meaning — his moments of life are almost spent — is exactly what the text says in context ('Here must I stay, and here my life must end').

anchor_text: I am your butt, and I abide your shot
summary: A 'butt' was a mound of earth set up as a target for archery practice; to 'abide' means to await or stand firm for. York is challenging his enemies to do their worst — 'I am your target, and I will not run from your attack.' The archery metaphor suits the martial setting.
detail: The butts were the standard archery ranges every English parish was required by law to maintain; 'butt' for a mark or target was everyday Elizabethan vocabulary. The phrase carries defiant double meaning: York names himself a stationary target but implies his enemies are merely at practice — not yet his equals in the field. Onions cites the archery sense as primary here.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'butt' (an archery target).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 436
Onions's Shakespeare Glossary documents 'butt' as an archery target; the citation is real and directly supports the archery-range sense described.

'Butt' as an archery target is the primary and correct Elizabethan sense; the secondary implication that York names his enemies 'merely at practice' is a plausible rhetorical reading, but lightly framed as suggestion rather than assertion, which keeps it defensible.

anchor_text: Phaethon hath tumbled from his car, And made an evening at the noontide prick
summary: Clifford mocks York's fall by comparing him to Phaethon, the reckless young man in Greek myth who borrowed his father's sun-chariot and lost control of it. Jove struck him with a thunderbolt before he could scorch the earth, plunging the world into sudden darkness — 'made an evening at the noontide prick' means brought darkness at the midday hour, when York's power was at its height.
detail: Shakespeare knew the Phaethon myth from Ovid's Metamorphoses 2.1-400 (widely read in Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567). The 'noontide prick' is the mark on a sundial for noon — the peak hour, when Phaethon's sun-chariot would be highest and brightest. Clifford's taunt is precise: York reached for the crown (the highest point) like Phaethon reaching for his father's fiery team, and was struck down before he could seize it. The image of overreaching ambition cut short is the scene's sharpest de casibus moment.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.1-400, trans. Arthur Golding (1567): Phaethon drives the sun-chariot and is destroyed by Jove's thunderbolt.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 440

Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 2, does contain the Phaethon story including Jupiter's thunderbolt; the cited range '2.1-400' is generous (core narrative ends around line 328, aftermath near 366) but encompasses the episode and is not fabricated.

Clifford's Phaethon taunt is well-supported: the myth (Ovid Met. 2) maps onto York's overreach for the crown, and 'noontide prick' as the sundial mark for noon is accurate Elizabethan usage; reading this as a de casibus moment is mainstream critical practice.

anchor_text: My ashes, as the phoenix, may bring forth A bird that will revenge upon you all
summary: York compares himself to the phoenix, the legendary bird of classical mythology that burns to ash every few hundred years and is reborn from its own ashes. He is prophesying that his sons will rise from his death to avenge him — a prophecy the rest of the play fulfills.
detail: The phoenix appears in Roman poetry (Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.392-407) and became a standard Renaissance emblem of resurrection, renewal, and undying lineage. York's phoenix is also a political image: his 'ashes' will produce an heir who will claim the throne. The prophecy is accurate — his son Edward wins the crown at Towton two acts later, and his son Richard eventually destroys the Lancastrian line entirely. Pliny the Elder (Natural History 10.2) also describes the phoenix as unique and self-regenerating; the image was a Tudor commonplace.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.392-407 (Golding 1567): the phoenix burns and rises renewed from its own ashes.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 10.2, on the unique self-regenerating phoenix.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 442

Ovid's phoenix passage is real but spans lines 391-417 in Book 15, not 392-407 as cited — the end-line is imprecise but the passage and its content are real; Pliny NH 10.2 is confirmed as the phoenix chapter and is supportive.

The phoenix-as-resurrection image is present in Ovid and Pliny and was a Tudor commonplace; York's prophetic application of it to his heirs (fulfilled by Edward's victory and Richard III's later arc) is grounded in the play's narrative and does not overread.

anchor_text: strives the woodcock with the gin. So doth the cony struggle in the net
summary: A 'gin' is a snare or trap (short for 'engine' in its old mechanical sense); a 'woodcock' was proverbially the most easily caught bird — considered stupid enough to walk into an obvious trap. A 'cony' is a rabbit. Clifford and Northumberland mock York's struggles as no better than a trapped bird or rabbit: he is already caught and his thrashing is futile.
detail: The woodcock-as-fool proverb is common in Elizabethan writing; its dullness was contrasted with the cleverness of the fox or the wary bird that escapes. Both images (woodcock in gin, cony in net) are paired proverbs of prey caught by their own unwary nature — Clifford and Northumberland divide them between themselves, each taking one bird, to double the taunt. OED records 'gin' (trap) in common use from the thirteenth century onward.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'gin' (trap, snare) and 'woodcock' (a proverbially foolish bird, hence a simpleton).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 468
Onions's Shakespeare Glossary documents 'gin' as a trap or snare and 'woodcock' as proverbially a foolish bird; the citation is real and directly supports the claims.

'Gin' as snare, 'woodcock' as proverbially foolish prey, and 'cony' as rabbit are all standard Elizabethan lexis accurately glossed; the reading that Clifford and Northumberland deliberately divide the two proverbs between them is a reasonable theatrical observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: raught at mountains with outstretched arms, Yet parted but the shadow with his hand
summary: 'Raught' is the past tense of 'reach' — an archaic form no longer used in modern English. Margaret mocks York as someone who 'reached for mountains' (the crown) but grasped only their shadow: he had nothing real, only the illusion of power. The image echoes the myth of Tantalus, though it may simply be a proverbial gesture.
detail: The form 'raught' for the past tense of 'reach' was already archaic in Shakespeare's day and lent a slightly formal, legal flavor. The mountain/shadow contrast draws on a long tradition of images for the gap between ambition and achievement: a mountain is real and immovable, a shadow shifts and vanishes. Margaret's contempt is sharpened by the fact that York DID reach the throne — and was then thrown off it — so 'shadow' is not merely mockery but a comment on how briefly and insecurely he held it.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'raught' (past tense of 'reach,' archaic past form current through the 16th and early 17th centuries).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 475
OED does document 'raught' as the archaic past tense of 'reach,' current through the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries; the citation is real and accurate.

'Raught' as archaic past tense of 'reach' is correct; the mountain/shadow contrast as a figure for the gap between ambition and achievement is what the text plainly says, and noting the irony that York did briefly attain the throne before being thrown off it is supported by prior dramatic context.

anchor_text: A crown for York! and, lords, bow low to him
summary: Margaret forces her captors to stage a grotesque mock coronation — a paper crown placed on the captive York's head while lords bow to him in sarcastic obeisance. The scene is drawn from Holinshed, though Shakespeare elaborates and intensifies it, making it the scene's central theatrical act and turning Margaret's cruelty into a dark parody of the royal ceremonies York claimed.
detail: Holinshed records that after the Battle of Wakefield the Lancastrians placed a paper crown on York's severed head before mounting it on the gates of York city. Shakespeare shifts the paper crown to a living ritual of humiliation before the execution, which is far more theatrically powerful and psychologically cruel — forcing York to wear the thing he died for, as a joke. The scene also deliberately inverts the royal ceremony at which a king is crowned, with Margaret playing the Archbishop and York forced to 'receive' the degraded crown. Historians note the paper crown as likely apocryphal; the theatrical impact was what mattered to Shakespeare.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): after Wakefield, York's severed head was mockingly crowned with paper and set on the gates of York.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 501
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record that York's head was mockingly crowned with paper and displayed on the gates of York after Wakefield; the citation is real and supportive.

The theatrical shift of the paper crown from post-mortem (Holinshed) to a living ritual of humiliation before execution is an accurate observation about how Shakespeare departs from the chronicle for dramatic effect, and is mainstream critical consensus.

anchor_text: She-wolf of France, but worse than wolves of France, Whose tongue more poisons than the adder's tooth
summary: York attacks Margaret with two stacked animal comparisons: the 'she-wolf of France' (a female wolf, emblem of predatory savagery — French wolves were proverbially fiercer than English ones) and the adder, whose bite was said to be poisonous. The phrase 'She-wolf of France' became the most memorable tag for Margaret across the trilogy and later in literature.
detail: French wolves were a genuine folk comparison — wolves had been extinct in England since the medieval period, so 'wolves of France' carried the automatic meaning of a fiercer and less familiar predator. The adder's 'tongue' poisons rather than its fang — a common Elizabethan confusion (adders were thought to sting with the tongue); it also sets up the rhetorical move of comparing Margaret's words to poison, which builds through the speech into the formal anaphora of TLN 535-543. 'She-wolf of France' was later applied by Thomas Gray to the historical Margaret of Anjou in his poem 'The Bard' (1757).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1886), s.v. 'adder' (tongue as the instrument of poison, a common Elizabethan confusion for the fang).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 518
Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference that covers 'adder' including the Elizabethan confusion of tongue for fang as the instrument of poison; the citation is real and supports the claim.

The she-wolf/adder pairing is plainly in the text; the note that adders were popularly thought to poison with the tongue (not the fang) is an accurate statement of Elizabethan folk belief; attributing the later 'She-wolf' tag to Thomas Gray's 'The Bard' (1757) is contextually appropriate without inflating its significance.

anchor_text: triumph, like an Amazonian trull, Upon their woes whom fortune captivates
summary: The Amazons were a nation of warrior women in classical mythology, famous for fighting men on equal or superior terms. To call Margaret an 'Amazonian trull' (a low woman who fights like an Amazon) is to insult her simultaneously as unnatural — a woman who acts like a warrior — and as sexually degraded. York is condemning not just her cruelty but her violation of expected female behavior.
detail: The Amazons appear in numerous classical sources (Herodotus, Plutarch's Life of Theseus); they were standard examples of women who had usurped the masculine role of war. In early modern Europe 'Amazon' could be applied with both admiration and horror to warrior queens. 'Trull' is a contemptuous word for a low woman or prostitute — Onions records it in common Elizabethan use. York's charge is that Margaret gloats over fallen men's suffering like a low Amazon: she has taken on the fighting role of a man but without honor or restraint. This ties to the scene's insistence that Margaret's face is 'impudent' and 'unchanging' — she shows no womanly softness.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911, rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'trull' (a low woman, a drab).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Theseus
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Theseus (North 1579) on the Amazons as warrior women, enemies of men.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 521
Onions covers 'trull' as a low woman; Plutarch's Life of Theseus (North 1579) does contain substantial material on the Amazons as warrior women; both citations are real and supportive.

'Trull' as a contemptuous term for a low woman and 'Amazonian' as denoting a woman who has usurped the masculine role of war are both accurate Elizabethan usages; the interpretation that York condemns Margaret simultaneously for cruelty and for gender transgression is exactly what the surrounding lines ('How ill-beseeming is it in thy sex') support.

anchor_text: Thy father bears the type of King of Naples, Of both the Sicils and Jerusalem, Yet not so wealthy as an English yeoman
summary: York mocks Margaret's father, Rene of Anjou, for bearing an impressive list of royal titles — King of Naples, King of Sicily, King of Jerusalem — none of which came with actual territory or income. 'Type' means title or style. A 'yeoman' was a middling English landowner; York is saying Rene's empty titles made him poorer in real wealth than a minor English farmer.
detail: Rene of Anjou (1409-1480) really did hold all three titles, all of them hereditary claims without practical control: he never governed Naples (expelled by Aragon in 1442), his Sicilian claim was nominal, and Jerusalem was a crusader-era honorific title still carried by European claimants centuries after the Crusades. His poverty was historically genuine — he is sometimes called 'the good king Rene' for his cultural patronage, which was all he could afford. 'Yeoman' denoted a freeholder below the rank of gentleman but above the laboring poor — prosperous by ordinary standards, absurdly so by comparison with a titular king of three kingdoms. Holinshed notes Rene's lack of wealth.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Rene of Anjou (Renier, Duke of Anjou), titled King of Naples, Sicily, and Jerusalem but without wealth or territory to match.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 528
Holinshed's Chronicles does mention Rene of Anjou's nominal titles (Naples, Sicily, Jerusalem) and his lack of real wealth; the citation is real and supports the historical claim.

'Type' as title or style is correct Elizabethan usage; Rene of Anjou's historical possession of all three titular claims (Naples, Sicily, Jerusalem) without real territory or income is historically accurate, and the yeoman comparison is what the text states plainly.

anchor_text: opposite to every good As the Antipodes are unto us, Or as the south to the Septentrion
summary: 'Antipodes' are the people or places diametrically opposite on the globe — literally those who stand with feet opposite to yours, on the other side of the earth. 'Septentrion' (or septentrione) means the north, from the Latin for the seven stars of the Great Bear. York is saying Margaret is as opposite to virtue as the far side of the earth or as south is to north: perfectly, absolutely contrary.
detail: The 'Antipodes' were a topic of lively Elizabethan curiosity and geographical dispute — since the Americas had been reached, the existence of people living upside-down on the other side was no longer merely theoretical. 'Septentrion' comes from the Latin septem (seven) + triones (draft-oxen or stars) — the seven stars of Ursa Major, the constellation that marks north. Shakespeare uses these learned compass-points to lend the insult a formal, rhetorical precision: the anaphora of the preceding lines ('T is beauty... T is virtue... T is government') builds to this pair of absolute-opposite images as its climax.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'Antipodes' (those inhabiting the opposite side of the globe) and 'septentrion' (the north; from Latin septentriones, the seven stars of the Great Bear).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 541
OED does contain entries for 'Antipodes' (those on the opposite side of the globe) and 'septentrion' (the north, from Latin septentriones); both citations are real and accurate.

'Antipodes' as those diametrically opposite on the globe and 'Septentrion' from Latin septem + triones (the seven stars of Ursa Major, hence north) are both accurately explained; the structural point that these geographical extremes cap the anaphoric series is a sound rhetorical observation.

anchor_text: O tiger's heart wrapp'd in a woman's hide
summary: This is among the most famous lines in the Henry VI plays, and the only line Shakespeare critics know was parodied by a contemporary: Robert Greene in 1592 attacked Shakespeare as an 'upstart crow' who had written 'tiger's heart wrapp'd in a player's hide,' closely echoing this line. York condemns Margaret's cruelty as a predatory animal's nature disguised inside a woman's body.
detail: The line's fame in its own time is confirmed by Robert Greene's posthumously published Groats-Worth of Wit (1592), which attacks 'Shake-scene' by parodying this exact line: 'tiger's heart wrapp'd in a player's hide' — a bitter quip that a mere actor had stolen the work of university-educated writers. That parody is the earliest known allusion to Shakespeare as a playwright. Tigers, in classical tradition (Pliny, Natural History 8.25; Ovid, Heroides 10.83), were the byword for savagery without mercy; 'Hyrcanian tigers' (from the region south of the Caspian Sea) were proverbially the most ferocious (see also TLN 562).

sources.name: Greene, Groats-Worth of Wit
sources.citation: Robert Greene, Groats-Worth of Wit (1592): 'tiger's heart wrapp'd in a player's hide' — a parody of this line, the earliest known allusion to Shakespeare as a playwright.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 8.25 (the tiger's proverbial ferocity).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 544

Greene's Groats-Worth of Wit (1592) is confirmed to contain the parody 'Tygers hart wrapt in a Players hyde,' and Pliny NH 8.25 does cover tigers and their Hyrcanian origins; both citations are real and supportive.

The Greene parody ('tiger's heart wrapp'd in a player's hide', Groats-Worth of Wit, 1592) as the earliest known contemporary allusion to Shakespeare as a playwright is established scholarly fact; the Hyrcanian tiger reference to Pliny and Ovid is accurate and consistent with the annotation at TLN 562.

anchor_text: These tears are my sweet Rutland's obsequies, And every drop cries vengeance for his death
summary: 'Obsequies' are funeral rites — the prayers, mourning, and ceremonies performed after a death. York is saying his tears are the only funeral service he can offer for his murdered son Rutland, since he has no time or freedom for a proper burial. The word is Latin-derived (obsequiae, from obsequi, to follow) and was common in formal Elizabethan usage.
detail: The absence of obsequies was a serious matter in both theology and social custom: without proper rites, the soul was thought to wander, and the family's honor was not properly marked. By weeping in the presence of his enemies York transforms his captive grief into a public ritual — his tears become, in the theatrical moment, a substitute ceremony that moves even the hostile Northumberland (TLN 557-558). The word also carries a slight legal sense (obsequium = service, compliance), giving the line a double meaning: these tears both mourn Rutland and serve his memory by seeking justice.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'obsequies' (funeral rites, the ceremonies performed at a burial; from Latin obsequiae).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 554
OED does document 'obsequies' as funeral rites derived from Latin obsequiae; the citation is real and supports the etymological and lexical claims.

The primary gloss ('obsequies' = funeral rites) is accurate, but the detail adds a secondary etymological claim that 'obsequium' (service/compliance) gives the line a 'slight legal sense' of seeking justice — this double meaning is not supported by standard Shakespearean commentary and stretches the Latin root beyond its normal semantic reach in this context.

anchor_text: ten times more, than tigers of Hyrcania
summary: Hyrcania was a region south of the Caspian Sea, in modern Iran and Turkmenistan, proverbially associated in classical literature with the most savage tigers. To be crueler than the 'tigers of Hyrcania' was the standard Latin way to say utterly merciless.
detail: The 'Hyrcanian tigers' appear in Virgil's Aeneid (4.366-368), where Dido accuses Aeneas of being nursed by Hyrcanian tigresses, and in Ovid. The phrase was a recognized classical tag for savagery beyond nature; Shakespeare uses it in Hamlet as well, where the Player calls Pyrrhus 'Hyrcanian beast' (2.2). York's insistence that Margaret and Clifford are 'ten times more' savage than these proverbial tigers is the speech's rhetorical climax, capping the series of animal comparisons (she-wolf, adder, tiger) that have structured the whole denunciation.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid
sources.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 4.366-368: Dido accuses Aeneas of being nursed by Hyrcanian tigresses — the standard classical locus for tigers as emblems of ferocity without mercy.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 562

Virgil's Aeneid 4.365-368 does contain Dido's accusation that Aeneas was nursed by Hyrcanian tigresses (Latin: 'Hyrcanaeque admorunt ubera tigres'); the citation at 4.366-368 is accurate and supportive.

Hyrcanian tigers as a classical tag for extreme ferocity (Virgil Aeneid 4.366-368; also Hamlet 2.2) is well-attested; the reading of this line as the rhetorical climax of the animal-comparison sequence (she-wolf, adder, tiger) is structurally accurate.

anchor_text: My soul to heaven, my blood upon your heads
summary: York's dying words echo a legal and biblical formula for pronouncing guilt on one's killers — 'your blood be upon your own head' means you are responsible for your own death. But inverted here ('my blood upon your heads'), it is a curse: the guilt of his murder will rest on Margaret and Clifford, who must answer for it before God. The formula comes from several Old Testament passages and recurs in the New Testament.
detail: The phrase 'blood upon your heads' draws on passages such as 2 Samuel 1:16 ('Thy blood be upon thy head') and Joshua 2:19, and most famously Matthew 27:25, where the crowd takes responsibility for Jesus's death ('His blood be on us and on our children'). In Shakespeare's histories the 'blood upon the head' formula is both a legal concept — the attribution of guilt — and a curse that fulfills itself: York's blood 'upon' his killers predicts the cycle of revenge the rest of the play delivers. Northumberland has already shown the compunction that is the first sign the curse will work.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: 2 Samuel 1:16 (Geneva 1599): 'Thy blood be upon thine own head'; Matthew 27:25: 'His blood be on us and on our children' — the standard biblical formula for assigning blood-guilt.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 575
2 Samuel 1:16 ('Thy blood be upon thy head') and Matthew 27:25 ('His blood be on us and on our children') are both real Geneva Bible passages that support the blood-guilt formula described.

The 'blood upon your heads' formula as a legal/biblical guilt-assignment phrase, citing 2 Samuel 1:16 and Matthew 27:25, is accurate; the reading that Northumberland's earlier compunction (TLN 557-558) is the first sign the curse begins to work is a defensible theatrical interpretation rather than an overreach.

anchor_text: Off with his head, and set it on York gates; So York may overlook the town of York
summary: After executions, the heads of traitors were commonly displayed on the gates of towns and on London Bridge as a warning and a mark of disgrace. Margaret's final act is to order York's head mounted on the Micklegate Bar, the principal gate of the city of York — a real historical action recorded by Holinshed. The grim pun ('York may overlook the town of York') is Margaret's parting cruelty.
detail: Holinshed records that after Wakefield, York's head was placed on the gates of York city wearing its paper crown, as a public display of Lancastrian victory and Yorkist humiliation. The practice of 'heading' — displaying the severed head of a traitor — was legally sanctioned in Elizabethan England; traitors' heads on London Bridge were a familiar sight to Shakespeare's audience. Micklegate Bar in York was the traditional gate through which royalty entered the city, making the choice of location a deliberate desecration. Shakespeare's punning last couplet ('So York may overlook the town of York') turns Margaret's real historical order into a bitter theatrical joke.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): after the Battle of Wakefield, York's head was mockingly crowned with paper and set on the gates of the city of York.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 586

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) records that York's head was crowned with paper and placed on the gates of the city of York after Wakefield; the citation is real and directly supports the historical claim.

Holinshed's record of York's head on the city gates with a paper crown is accurately cited, and the identification of Micklegate Bar as the traditional royal entry gate (making its use here a deliberate desecration) is historically sound; the pun on 'York/York' is plainly in the text.

anchor_text: Clifford's and Northumberland's pursuit
summary: Edward and Richard do not know whether their father, the Duke of York, survived the Lancastrian rout at Wakefield. Lord Clifford (the son of the Clifford slain at the First Battle of St Albans) and Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, led the Lancastrian forces that pursued the fleeing Yorkists after Wakefield.
detail: The Battle of Wakefield (30 December 1460) was a crushing Lancastrian victory in which the Duke of York was killed. Holinshed records that the earls of Northumberland and Wiltshire, alongside Clifford, were among the commanders of the force that overwhelmed York's army. Clifford's personal vendetta against the house of York — his father was killed at St Albans — gives his pursuit a ferocity that distinguishes it from ordinary military pursuit. The scene opens, then, with Edward and Richard in ignorance of a disaster the audience has just witnessed.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Wakefield, 30 December 1460.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 590
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does record Clifford and Northumberland among the Lancastrian commanders at Wakefield, 30 December 1460; the historical claim is accurate and the source supports it.

The scene opens with Edward and Richard genuinely ignorant of York's fate after Wakefield; the identification of Clifford (whose father fell at St Albans) and Northumberland as the Lancastrian pursuers is supported by Holinshed and dramatized in the preceding act.

anchor_text: bore him in the thickest troop As doth a lion in a herd of neat
summary: Richard compares his father's charge through the Lancastrian troops to a lion cutting through a herd of cattle. 'Neat' is an archaic word for cattle, especially oxen or cows. The simile frames York as a lordly predator surrounded by inferior, panic-stricken beasts — a standard image of heroic courage in Elizabethan martial poetry.
detail: The lion-among-cattle comparison was a classical commonplace for a hero in battle. It appears in Homer's Iliad (e.g. Iliad 5.161, 11.172) and repeatedly in Virgil. Richard piles up two such similes — lion among neat, then bear surrounded by dogs — to elevate his father into legend even as he privately grieves. The rhetorical figure is a simile (extended comparison using 'as' or 'like').

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'neat' n.2: 'Cattle, oxen; now only dialectal or archaic.' Also Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'neat.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 600
OED s.v. 'neat' n.2 and Schmidt s.v. 'neat' are real, standard lexicographical entries confirming the archaic meaning 'cattle/oxen'; the lion-simile claim is supported.

The lion-among-cattle simile is explicitly in the text ('as doth a lion in a herd of neat'), 'neat' as archaic for cattle is standard OED usage, and the Homeric/Virgilian pedigree for hero-as-lion in battle is well established — the annotation does not overclaim.

anchor_text: morning opes her golden gates And takes her farewell of the glorious sun
summary: Richard personifies the dawn as a woman opening her 'golden gates' to bid farewell to the sun. 'Younker' (line 611) is an archaic term for a young gallant or fine gentleman, so the dawn is 'trimmed' (dressed up) like a fashionable young man on the way to meet his lover.
detail: The image draws on the classical conceit of Aurora (the dawn goddess) opening the gates of heaven for the sun — Ovid's Metamorphoses repeatedly personifies the dawn in such terms. Shakespeare fuses the mythological picture with contemporary social observation (the preening 'younker') to produce a sunrise description that is briefly lyrical before the Messenger's terrible news arrives. 'Younker' or 'younker' = a young man of fashion (Dutch jonker, 'young lord'); Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'younker'.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.112-114 (Aurora opening the doors of her palace for Phaethon's ride); Golding's 1567 English translation.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'younker': 'a young gallant or fashionable gentleman.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 608
Ovid Metamorphoses 2.112-114 does describe Aurora opening her bright doors/gates as Phaethon prepares to ride the chariot; OED s.v. 'younker' is a real entry — both sources support the claims.

The Aurora/golden-gates conceit is plausible, but the annotation conflates two distinct things: the dawn 'taking her farewell of the sun' is actually an unusual reversal of Aurora as the sun's herald (she normally precedes, not bids farewell to, the sun), and the Ovid Met. 2.112-114 parallel (Aurora opening doors for Phaethon) is not a close match to this image; the 'younker' gloss is accurate but the overall classical framing overstates the specificity.

anchor_text: Dazzle mine eyes, or do I see three suns
summary: Edward sees three distinct suns in the sky that gradually merge into one. This is an atmospheric phenomenon called a 'parhelion' (or 'sun dog') — a natural optical effect where ice crystals in the air cause two bright spots to appear beside the real sun, creating the appearance of three suns. Shakespeare takes the episode from Holinshed, who reports that Edward IV claimed to have seen it before the Battle of Mortimer's Cross (1461).
detail: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), records: 'In the morning before the battell, at the sun rising, three sunnes appeared in the firmament, shining full cleare, and immediatlie ioyned altogither into one.' Edward IV adopted the 'Sun in Splendour' as his personal badge — directly commemorating this omen. Edward's interpretation (lines 620-627), that the three suns represent himself and his two brothers George and Richard now merging their powers into one, is his on-the-spot political reading of a natural sign. The badge of the 'sunne in his splendour' remained central to Yorkist heraldry and appears on the livery of Edward's retainers throughout the play.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Mortimer's Cross, February 1461.

anchor_text: I'll draw it as apparent to the crown
summary: 'Apparent' here is a legal term meaning 'heir apparent' — the person who is the undoubted, next-in-line heir to the throne, whose claim cannot be set aside by the birth of another heir (as opposed to 'heir presumptive'). anchor_text: Darraign your battle, for they are at hand
summary: 'Darraign' (also spelled 'deraign') is a Middle English military term meaning to draw up, set in order, or prepare an army for battle. It comes from Old French 'derainier' (to justify, put in order). By the 1590s it was already archaic; the messenger's use of it signals the formal, quasi-legal language of challenges and counter-challenges that frames this pre-battle parley.

anchor_text: Now, perjur'd Henry, wilt thou kneel for grace
summary: Edward calls Henry 'perjur'd' — oath-breaking — because in Act 1 Scene 1 Henry had solemnly agreed to let the Yorkist line succeed him after his death, disinheriting his own son. His subsequent change of mind (engineered by Margaret) and the parliamentary act that put the prince back in the succession (TLN 888-889) are what Edward calls perjury. Henry had sworn an oath before Parliament; breaking it was both a moral and a constitutional act of bad faith.

anchor_text: Go, rate thy minions, proud insulting boy
summary: 'Rate' means to scold, berate, or rebuke. 'Minions' are favorites or hangers-on — here Margaret contemptuously dismisses Edward's companions (George, Richard, Warwick) as mere lackeys. The charge of being a 'proud insulting boy' plays on Edward's youth and lack of royal dignity; 'insulting' in Elizabethan usage could mean 'triumphing insolently over' (from Latin 'insultare,' to leap upon), not just using offensive words.
