sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'rate' vb.: to scold, chide; and s.v. 'minion': a favourite, a dependant; a creature of another's will.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 881

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), is a real standard reference and does carry entries for 'rate' (to scold, chide) and 'minion' (favourite, dependant); the definitions given accurately reflect Onions's documented coverage.

'Rate' as scold and 'minions' as favorites/hangers-on are standard Elizabethan usages confirmed by Onions; the etymological note on 'insulting' from Latin 'insultare' (to leap upon, triumph insolently) is correct and the sense is well-supported in the period.

anchor_text: Are you there, butcher?--O, I cannot speak
summary: Richard of Gloucester (the future Richard III) is so enraged at the sight of Clifford that he can barely form words. He calls him 'butcher' for the murder of York's youngest son Rutland (1.3), a child, and for helping kill York himself. Clifford freely admits both kills and adds 'yet not satisfied' (TLN 896) — meaning he has not yet had enough revenge for his own father's death at St Albans. 'Crook-back' (TLN 893) is Clifford's counter-jibe at Richard's physical deformity, an insult that will follow him through the play and into Richard III.
detail: The exchange crystallizes the play's cycle of blood-vengeance. Clifford killed Rutland to avenge his own father (slain by York at the first battle of St Albans); Richard will hunt Clifford throughout this battle to avenge Rutland and York; and Richard himself will eventually murder Henry and his son, adding new debts to the cycle. Clifford's 'crook-back' is the play's bluntest acknowledgement of Richard's deformity, which he will later weaponize in his self-defining 3.2 soliloquy.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Clifford's killing of the Earl of Rutland at Wakefield (1460) and his killing of the Duke of York.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 892

Holinshed (1587) records Clifford's killing of the Earl of Rutland at Wakefield (1460) and his role in York's death; the reference to the first battle of St Albans (where Clifford's father was killed) is accurate historical context.

The identification of Richard's fury as directed at Clifford for killing Rutland (1.3) and York, and 'crook-back' as Clifford's jibe at Richard's deformity, are all textually explicit; the connection forward to Richard's 3.2 soliloquy is a legitimate intertextual observation, not an overreach.

anchor_text: like a foul misshapen stigmatic, Mark'd by the destinies to be avoided
summary: Margaret calls Richard a 'stigmatic' — a person branded or marked by nature as a sign of divine displeasure or predestination to evil. A 'stigma' (Greek: a brand or mark) was the mark of a slave or criminal; applied to Richard's physical deformity, the word taps into Elizabethan belief that visible deformity could signal moral corruption within. The phrase 'mark'd by the destinies' adds a classical gloss (the Fates who assign each person's lot at birth), intensifying the insult as cosmological condemnation.
detail: The slander is pointed partly because Richard will later embrace and weaponize it: in his 3.2 soliloquy he attributes his ambition precisely to being 'cheated of feature' — his deformity becomes his motive for villainy. The Elizabethan physiognomic tradition (reading character from body) is invoked here as a smear, but it is one Richard will own. 'As venom toads or lizards' dreadful stings' picks up the Elizabethan lore that toads and lizards were venomous; toads in particular were associated with witchcraft and corruption in popular and literary culture.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'stigmatic' n. 2: 'One who bears a stigma or mark (of disgrace); one branded or marked; hence, a person having physical deformity regarded as a sign of evil or divine disfavour.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 933

The OED does record 'stigmatic' n. with a sense covering a person bearing a mark of physical deformity regarded as a sign of disgrace or divine disfavour; the definition quoted is consistent with documented OED senses.

'Stigmatic' as one branded by nature as a sign of divine disfavor is the established Elizabethan sense (OED n.2), and the physiognomic tradition linking deformity to moral corruption is well-documented; the note that Richard will embrace this framing in his 3.2 soliloquy is sound and not anachronistic.

anchor_text: Iron of Naples hid with English gilt
summary: Richard insults Margaret by attacking her father's rank. Her father, Rene of Anjou, held the grand title 'King of Naples and Jerusalem' but held almost no actual territory — he was famously 'the king of nothing.' 'Iron' means base metal; 'gilt' (gold plating over inferior metal) means a false, shiny surface hiding worthlessness. The image calls Margaret a cheap imitation of a queen, her royal blood fraudulent beneath the coating.
detail: Rene I of Anjou (1409-1480) claimed the kingdoms of Naples, Jerusalem, Aragon, and Hungary, which gave him magnificent title but no real power — he lost Naples to Alfonso of Aragon in 1442 and Sicily remained nominal. 'Extraught' (TLN 939) is an archaic past participle of 'extract,' meaning 'descended' or 'derived.' The insult continues: Margaret's 'base-born heart' is disclosed by her own aggressive 'tongue.' The whole passage is a genealogical attack mounted by Richard (whose own royal blood is impeccable) against Margaret's lowly actual origins as the daughter of a title-rich but territory-poor French duke.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the marriage of Henry VI to Margaret of Anjou and on the weak position of her father Rene, nominal king of Naples and Jerusalem. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'extraught': derived, descended (archaic past participle of 'extract').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 936

Holinshed (1587) covers Henry VI's marriage to Margaret of Anjou and Rene of Anjou's weak territorial position; Rene did hold the nominal title 'King of Naples and Jerusalem' while losing actual control of Naples to Alfonso of Aragon in 1442 — all claims confirmed.

The 'iron gilded' image as base metal beneath a false gold surface applied to Margaret's fraudulent royal claim via her father Rene's nominal kingship is textually grounded; Rene's loss of Naples to Alfonso of Aragon (1442) and his merely titular holdings are historical fact, and 'extraught' as archaic past participle of 'extract' is correct.

anchor_text: A wisp of straw were worth a thousand crowns To make this shameless callat know herself
summary: A 'callat' (or 'callet') was a coarse term for a scolding, immoral woman or prostitute. Edward uses it as the ultimate social put-down for a queen whom he considers beneath her station. 'A wisp of straw' was a bundle of straw sometimes carried as a badge of shame for nagging or quarrelsome women — so his image is of strapping a dunce-marker on Margaret to humiliate her publicly into self-awareness.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), s.v. 'callet' (also 'callat'): a lewd woman, drab, scold. Compare Othello 4.2.120 and The Winter's Tale 2.3.90 for the same term.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 941

Onions (1911) and the cross-play usage of 'callat/callet' in The Winter's Tale (2.3) and Othello are confirmed, but the specific line number 'Othello 4.2.120' cannot be verified — the word does appear in 4.2 but line numbering varies by edition and '120' may be inaccurate.

'Callet'/'callat' as a coarse term for a scolding or immoral woman is correct (Onions); the 'wisp of straw' as a publicly humiliating badge for a scold is a real Elizabethan custom and is not invented; the speaker attribution to Edward (not Richard) matches TLN 941-942.

anchor_text: Helen of Greece was fairer far than thou, Although thy husband may be Menelaus
summary: Edward compares Margaret to Helen of Troy, the most beautiful woman in the classical world — but only to insult her: 'Helen was fairer than you, though your husband (Henry) is in the same position as Helen's wronged husband Menelaus.' Helen's elopement with Paris of Troy drove her husband Menelaus to war and destroyed Troy; Edward says Margaret's behavior has done the same damage to England's king. 'Agamemnon's brother' is Menelaus — Agamemnon (king of Mycenae and leader of the Greek expedition) was his older brother.
detail: The analogy is structured: Margaret is an unfaithful or destructive wife (like Helen), Henry is the wronged king-husband (like Menelaus), and the wars are the result. Edward is also attacking Margaret's French origins: just as Helen was a foreign woman who wrecked a great kingdom, so Margaret came from France and wrecked England. The detail 'His father revell'd in the heart of France' (TLN 947) sharpens the irony: Henry V conquered France; his son Henry VI lost it by marrying a Frenchwoman who brought 'sedition on his crown at home' (TLN 955).

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 3 (Helen, wife of Menelaus, carried off by Paris, causing the Trojan War). Agamemnon as Menelaus's brother: Iliad 1.7.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 943

Homer, Iliad Book 3, does present Helen, Menelaus, and their conflict with Paris; Agamemnon's brotherhood with Menelaus (as sons of Atreus) is established throughout the Iliad — the citation 'Iliad 1.7' for the brotherhood is imprecise (1.7 concerns Agamemnon and Achilles, not the brothers), but the broader Iliad 3 citation is accurate and supportive.

The Helen/Menelaus analogy (Margaret:Henry :: Helen:Menelaus, destructive foreign wife wrecks a great king) is textually explicit at TLN 943-946 and the identification of Agamemnon as Menelaus's brother is correct; the extension to Henry VI losing France as the 'Trojan War' parallel is interpretively sound and not overread.

anchor_text: His father revell'd in the heart of France, And tam'd the king, and made the dauphin stoop
summary: Edward is referring to Henry V, Henry VI's father, who defeated the French at Agincourt (1415), captured vast territories, and forced the French king to sign the Treaty of Troyes (1420) — making Henry V heir to the French crown and putting the French Dauphin out of the succession. 'Revell'd' does not mean partied here; it means triumphed or held glorious sway. Edward's point is that Henry VI squandered his father's conquests by marrying beneath him (Margaret of Anjou was the daughter of a near-powerless French duke).

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry V's conquest of France and the Treaty of Troyes (1420), by which the French king Charles VI made Henry heir to France and the Dauphin was disinherited.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 947

Holinshed (1587) covers Henry V's French conquests and the Treaty of Troyes (1420), by which the French king made Henry heir to France and the Dauphin was disinherited — all claims are accurate and well-sourced.

'Revell'd' glossed as 'triumphed / held glorious sway' rather than 'partied' is the correct contextual reading; the reference to Henry V, Agincourt, and the Treaty of Troyes is accurate, and the contrast with Henry VI's marriage to Margaret as squandering those gains is the explicit argumentative logic of TLN 947-955.

anchor_text: Forspent with toil, as runners with a race
summary: 'Forspent' means utterly exhausted, spent out — the prefix 'for-' intensifies 'spent' to total depletion. Warwick enters the battle having fought so hard that he compares himself to a runner who has finished a race, unable to go on without rest.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'forspent' (also 'forespent'): 'completely exhausted, worn out' (attested from the 14th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 975

The gloss 'utterly exhausted, spent out' is the standard OED sense and fits the context of Warwick collapsing after battle; the runner simile in the same line confirms it.

anchor_text: Edward's sun is clouded
summary: Edward puns on 'sun' and 'son': the sun in splendor (a radiant golden sun-burst) was the principal heraldic badge of the house of York, so a clouded sun means both bad weather on the battlefield and the York cause in eclipse. The pun recurs throughout the plays of the first tetralogy as a mark of Yorkist identity.

Edward traces his use of the sun badge to a vision of three suns at 2.1.25-40 of this play, and in Richard III 1.1 Richard famously opens with the same pun in reverse ('Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun of York'). Heraldically the York device is the 'sun in its splendour,' a golden sun with wavy and straight rays, which Edward IV used on coinage and in royal display. At Towton the Yorkists were on the losing side for much of the day before the wind shifted and the tide turned, so 'clouded' has a literal meteorological reference to the snowstorm in which the battle was fought.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): the Battle of Towton, 29 March 1461, fought in snow and wind; the Yorkist sun-badge and Edward's vision of three suns before the battle.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'sun': notes the York heraldic pun across the Henry VI plays and Richard III.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 981

The sun/son pun and the Yorkist heraldic sun badge are well-established Shakespearean devices confirmed by the parallel in Richard III 1.1.1-2, and the meteorological 'clouded' reading suits the Towton snowstorm setting; the note that Warwick is 'kneeling beside' Edward appears only in the detail field and refers to a moment later in the scene, not to TLN 981 itself.

anchor_text: Thy brother's blood the thirsty earth hath drunk, Broach'd with the steely point
summary: 'Broach'd' means pierced or tapped open — the same word used for broaching (opening) a cask of wine. Richard tells Warwick that their brother Montague has been run through by Clifford's lance, his blood spilled into the earth like wine from a tapped barrel. The image makes the battlefield's absorption of blood viscerally concrete.

Shakespeare uses it several times for death by weapon, always carrying the liquid-from-vessel undertone. Here the parallel structure — earth 'drinks' blood that has been 'broached' by a lance — makes the earth itself a consuming vessel. The brother in question is John Neville, Marquess of Montague, Warwick's brother, who fights on the Yorkist side at Towton. Richard's report of his death is Shakespeare's invention; historically Montague survived Towton and was killed at Barnet in 1471.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'broach' v.: sense 3, 'to pierce, stab'; sense 1, 'to tap (a cask)' — both current in the 16th century.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587): Montague's role at Towton and eventual death at Barnet (1471).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 989
OED s.v. 'broach' confirms senses of both piercing and tapping a cask, attested in the 16th century; Holinshed correctly records Montague's role at Towton and death at Barnet (1471).

'Broach'd' as 'pierced/tapped open' carrying the wine-cask undertone is the standard OED sense and fits the earth-as-vessel image; the note that Montague's death at Towton is Shakespeare's invention (he died at Barnet 1471) is accurate and appropriate.

anchor_text: Forslow no longer; make we hence amain
summary: 'Forslow' means to delay, waste time, or be slow about something — an urgent command to stop lingering. 'Amain' means with full speed, at full force. George is rallying the group: stop stalling, let us leave from here at top speed.
detail: 'Forslow' (also 'forslack') is a now-archaic verb combining the intensifying prefix 'for-' with 'slow' to mean deliberate delay or dallying; it appears in Spenser's Faerie Queene and in other Elizabethan texts in military urgency contexts. 'Amain' derives from 'main' in the sense of 'full strength or force' and means with all speed, or with full sail — a nautical and military term for maximum momentum. Both words belong to the register of battlefield command, stressing decisive, rapid action, and their compression into a single short line enacts the urgency George is demanding.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'forslow' (also 'forslack'): 'to delay, be dilatory, neglect' (attested 14th-17th century); OED s.v. 'amain': 'with full force or speed' (16th-17th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1030

OED entries for 'forslow' and 'amain' are real and match the definitions given; 'forslow' is confirmed in Spenser's Faerie Queene (1596) and other Elizabethan texts, and 'amain' as 'with full force or speed' is well attested.
'Forslow' as 'delay/dally' and 'amain' as 'with full speed/force' are both accurately defined with solid OED attestation; the etymology of 'amain' from 'main' (strength) is correct.

anchor_text: I have singled thee alone
summary: 'Singled' is a hunting term: to single an animal is to cut it off from the herd or pack so it can be pursued alone. Richard is casting himself as a hunter and Clifford as the prey separated for the kill.
detail: The hunting vocabulary is deliberate and sustained: the scene closes with Richard demanding to 'hunt this wolf to death' (TLN 1043). Elizabethan audiences familiar with field sports would hear the full predator-prey logic at once. The verb also implies that Richard has maneuvered tactically to isolate Clifford from the broader melee — 'excursions' in the stage direction signals the surrounding battle chaos through which Richard has tracked his quarry.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'single' v., sense 4: 'To separate (an animal, or a person) from others; to pick out and pursue singly' (earliest hunting usage c. 1530).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1031
OED s.v. 'single' v. sense 4 is a real and well-attested entry documenting the hunting usage; the earliest citation date and gloss cited are consistent with the OED's documented record for this verb.

The hunting sense of 'singled' is textually supported by the scene's sustained predator-prey frame (chase, wolf, hunt) and Richard's deliberate isolation of Clifford from the surrounding battle melee.

anchor_text: single out some other chase; For I myself will hunt this wolf to death
summary: 'Chase' is a hunting term for the quarry being pursued, and calling Clifford a 'wolf' casts him as vermin that must be destroyed rather than an honorable opponent. The language completes the hunting frame Richard opened at TLN 1031 ('singled thee alone'), framing his personal vendetta as a righteous extermination.
detail: Wolves had been effectively extinct in southern England by the late medieval period but survived in the north; they were a byword for treacherous, bloodthirsty predators. Elizabethan law classified wolves with vermin that could be killed on sight, with no rules of chivalric engagement. By calling Clifford a wolf rather than a knight, Richard denies him any claim to honorable combat and licenses his own obsessive pursuit outside the normal conventions of war. The dismissal of Warwick ('single out some other chase') also quietly establishes Richard as a loner who acts outside the chain of command — a trait that defines him throughout the play and into Richard III. Holinshed uses 'wolf' and 'butcher' as standard epithets for Clifford (Chronicles, 1587, III.657).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'chase' n.2, sense 3: 'The animal or game pursued in hunting' (in use from c. 1300).

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles of England (1587 ed.), vol. III, p. 657: Clifford styled 'the Butcher' for his Wakefield killings; wolves as vermin in Elizabethan statute law.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1042

OED 'chase' n.2 sense 3 is real and credible; the Holinshed vol. III p. 657 page reference is unverifiable in the 1587 edition without direct access, and the appended claim about wolves in 'Elizabethan statute law' is unsourced within the citation, but the Clifford 'Butcher' epithet is historically attested in Holinshed via Hall.

All three interpretive moves — 'chase' as quarry, 'wolf' as vermin outside chivalric norms, and Richard's dismissal of Warwick as a loner trait — are grounded directly in the scene text and are mainstream readings.

anchor_text: this battle fares like to the morning's war
summary: Henry opens with a sustained simile comparing the balance of battle to a sea driven by wind and tide, 'now one the better, then another best,' with neither side winning ('equal poise'). The extended comparison is an example of the rhetorical figure called 'traductio' or sustained analogy; it runs for thirteen lines before Henry names the battle at all. The device signals his detachment — he watches and meditates rather than fights.
detail: The rhetorical amplification is deliberate: Henry is excluded from the fighting by Margaret and Clifford ('Have chid me from the battle,' TLN 1060), so all he can do is describe. The sea-and-wind image is a classical topic for indecisive struggle (compare Virgil, Aeneid 10.356-361, the simile of tide and opposing wind); Shakespeare gives it political weight — a kingdom 'at equal poise' is a kingdom paralysed. The word 'fell' (TLN 1056, meaning fierce or cruel) is archaic; see note below.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'fell' and 'poise'.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Battle of Towton, 29 March 1461 — the battle dramatized in this act.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1044

Aeneid 10.356-361 is a real and relevant simile of evenly-matched winds in battle (anceps pugna diu); the annotation calls it a 'tide and opposing wind' simile but the passage is wind-vs-wind with sea as bystander — a slight misdescription but the citation genuinely supports an 'equal poise' battle simile; Schmidt lexicon and Holinshed on Towton are credible standard references.

The extended sea-and-wind simile is plainly present in the text (TLN 1044-1056), the identification of 'fell' as archaic for 'fierce' is correct, and reading Henry's detachment as the motive for the descriptive amplification is mainstream and defensible; calling the device 'traductio' is a loose but not wrong label for sustained analogy.

anchor_text: Here on this molehill will I sit me down
summary: A molehill is a tiny mound of earth thrown up by a burrowing mole — the opposite of a throne or a battlefield command post. The image mirrors an earlier scene: in Act 1 Margaret crowned the captured York with a paper crown and made him stand on a molehill to be mocked. Now Henry sits on a molehill while his queen fights the battle he is too gentle to fight. The repeated symbol frames both rivals as kings stripped of real power.
detail: The echo of York's molehill humiliation (1.4) is structural: where Margaret forced York onto a molehill to humiliate him before killing him, Henry voluntarily retreats to a molehill, excluded from the fight by the same Margaret. The Wars-of-the-Roses cycle of humiliation and revenge runs through this symbol. Holinshed describes Henry VI as unfit for warfare and frequently set aside by his queen and commanders; Shakespeare crystallises that historical characterisation in this single prop. The molehill also sets up the extraordinary theatrical spectacle that follows — the king as passive, lamenting witness rather than active agent.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VI's passive role at Towton and the battle's conduct under Margaret and Clifford.

sources.name: Hall, Union
sources.citation: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548), on the same.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1057
Holinshed (1587) and Hall (1548) are both real, well-attested sources for Henry VI's passive conduct at Towton and his displacement by Margaret as battlefield commander.

The structural echo of York's molehill in 1.4 is a genuine and widely noted piece of staging symmetry, and reading Henry's voluntary retreat as the mirror-image of York's forced humiliation is standard critical reading; the Holinshed context on Henry's passive role is accurate.

anchor_text: O God! methinks it were a happy life, To be no better than a homely swain
summary: Henry wishes he were 'a homely swain' — a plain shepherd — rather than a king. 'Homely' means simple and unpretentious (not ugly), and 'swain' is a shepherd or farm labourer. He imagines carving sundials ('dials'), counting the hours, tending his flock, and dying in quiet old age. This is the 'pastoral' convention: a literary tradition, rooted in classical poetry, that imagined rural life as a blessed escape from the anxieties of courts and power.
detail: The pastoral speech is the most extended lyric passage in the play and one of the most celebrated in the Henry VI trilogy. Henry's idealized shepherd life — measured time, seasonal work, a quiet grave — is the deliberate opposite of everything a monarch experiences: treachery, 'care, mistrust, and treason' (TLN 1097). The speech derives from a classical topos (Virgil, Eclogues; Horace, Epodes 2 — 'Beatus ille,' 'Happy is the man who...') but also reflects Henry's known historical piety and distaste for warfare. Shakespeare's audiences would have recognized the pastoral lyric as a genre; its placement here, in the middle of the bloodiest battle in the play, heightens the pathos. 'Ean' (TLN 1079) means to give birth (of sheep); 'dials' (TLN 1067) are sundials.

anchor_text: To carve out dials quaintly, point by point
summary: 'Dials' are sundials — discs or faces marked with hours so a shadow tells the time. 'Quaintly' means skillfully and with delicate craft (not oddly). The shepherd Henry imagines sitting on a hillside carving a sundial, then watching it count the hours of a life measured in shepherd's tasks instead of battles and treasons.

anchor_text: So many weeks ere the poor fools will ean
summary: 'Ean' (also spelled 'yean') means to give birth, used specifically of sheep and goats. 'Fools' here is an affectionate term for the ewes and their young — a common rural endearment in Shakespeare's time, not a term of contempt. Henry imagines counting the weeks until his flock lambs.

anchor_text: From London by the king was I press'd forth; My father, being the Earl of Warwick's man, Came on the part of York
summary: To be 'pressed' (conscripted) meant to be forcibly enrolled into military service by royal authority, without choice. The Son was pressed by the Lancastrian king, his father was pressed by Warwick (a Yorkist at this point in the play), and so father and son ended up on opposite sides of the same battle without knowing it. This is not family treachery but the arbitrary machinery of civil war — the same system that randomly divided families and set them against each other.
detail: The 'press' (forced military levy) was a real Elizabethan grievance; men could be seized off the streets for military service. The scene dramatizes its human cost with surgical precision: neither man chose to fight the other, and neither knew the other was on the opposite side. The detail that the father served 'the Earl of Warwick's man' places the scene at Towton, where Warwick fought on the Yorkist side (he would later switch to Lancaster). Holinshed records the enormous conscript forces at Towton — tens of thousands pressed from across the country.

The 'press' as forced conscription is historically accurate and OED-supported; the reading that the divided allegiance is the machinery of civil war rather than family treachery is clearly the play's own framing ('unwares,' 'I knew not') and is not an over-reading.

anchor_text: Whiles lions war and battle for their dens, Poor harmless lambs abide their enmity
summary: Henry compares the warring nobles to lions fighting over their dens and the common people to lambs caught in the crossfire. The lion was the heraldic symbol of the English crown; the lamb was the symbol of innocent suffering (and of Christ). The contrast packages the scene's whole argument: the great destroy each other and the innocent suffer for it. The figure is a 'simile' turned 'maxim' — a general truth illustrated by an animal parallel.

The lion-as-heraldic-crown and lamb-as-innocent-suffering contrast is a clean and mainstream reading; 'abide' meaning 'suffer the consequences of' is accurate, and the claim does not overreach the text.

anchor_text: What stratagems, how fell, how butcherly, Erroneous, mutinous, and unnatural
summary: 'Stratagems' in Shakespeare almost always means acts of violence, slaughter, or treachery — not just clever plans. 'Fell' means fierce, savage, cruel. 'Butcherly' means like a butcher — with brutal, indiscriminate killing. 'Erroneous' here means straying from right and law (its root sense from Latin 'errare,' to wander). 'Unnatural' is key: killing one's own child violates the order of nature itself, which the speech insists this 'deadly quarrel' now routinely 'begets.'

anchor_text: The red rose and the white are on his face, The fatal colours of our striving houses
summary: Henry reads the dead son's face as an emblem of the two rival houses: the red blood represents Lancaster (the red rose), the pale cheeks represent York (the white rose). The rose badges are the play's central symbols for the civil war — York and Lancaster each claimed a rose as their heraldic emblem. Henry's image turns the killed boy's body into a living coat of arms — a piece of symbolic stagecraft that compresses the whole war into a single human face.
detail: The red and white rose as Lancastrian and Yorkist badges were genuine, though the 'Wars of the Roses' as a collective name was only popularised centuries after the events (see the wars-of-the-roses card). Edward Hall's chronicle, the Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548), was named for the rose symbols and was Shakespeare's major source alongside Holinshed. Henry's 'Wither one rose, and let the other flourish! / If you contend, a thousand lives must wither' is an unusual moment of political clarity for the otherwise passive king.

sources.name: Hall, Union
sources.citation: Edward Hall, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York (1548): the chronicle named for the rose emblems of both houses.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Lancastrian and Yorkist badges.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1140

Reading the dead son's red blood and pale cheeks as Lancastrian red and Yorkist white is the play's own explicit equation (Henry states it directly), and the note about the collective name 'Wars of the Roses' being later popularized is a useful and accurate caution.

anchor_text: How will my mother, for a father's death
summary: Shakespeare structures three parallel laments — the Son (TLN 1146-1147), the Father (TLN 1148-1149), and the King (TLN 1150-1151) — each beginning 'How will...' and ending with 'ne'er be satisfied.' Then a second set mirrors it: 'Was ever son...', 'Was ever father...', 'Was ever king...' (TLN 1152-1154). This is the rhetorical figure 'anaphora' (repeated opening words) combined with 'tricolon' (a set of three parallel units). The strict formal symmetry turns private grief into a public ceremony of mourning and makes the scene feel ritualistic rather than realistic.
detail: The triadic structure is almost choral — the three figures lament in turn, like a Greek tragedy where the chorus speaks in response to the protagonist. Shakespeare may have been influenced by the tradition of the 'planctus' (lamentation) in medieval religious drama, where formalized grief was expressed in strict parallel repetition. The scene was almost certainly intended as a set-piece: three actors, formally arranged, speaking in counterpoint while the king weeps between them. The artifice is deliberate — it distances the horror so the audience can contemplate its meaning rather than just react to it.

sources.name: Lanham, Handbook of Rhetorical Terms
sources.citation: Richard A. Lanham, A Handlist of Rhetorical Terms, 2nd ed. (1991), s.v. 'anaphora' and 'tricolon.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1146

The anaphora ('How will...', 'Was ever...') and tricolon structure are plainly present in the text and the identification of the devices is accurate; the comparison to a Greek choral lament and the medieval 'planctus' tradition is a defensible (if unverified) scholarly suggestion appropriately hedged with 'may have been influenced.'

anchor_text: These arms of mine shall be thy winding-sheet; My heart, sweet boy, shall be thy sepulchre
summary: A 'winding-sheet' was the cloth a corpse was wrapped in for burial — a shroud. 'Sepulchre' is a burial chamber or tomb. The Father says his arms holding his dead son will serve as the shroud, and his heart as the tomb. He cannot bury his son properly; his own body becomes the grave. The speech condenses the whole catastrophe of civil war into the image of a father carrying a son he cannot bury.

'Winding-sheet' as burial shroud and 'sepulchre' as tomb are both correct, and the reading of the Father's body becoming a surrogate grave is directly supported by the text's own metaphor; the gloss does not overreach.

anchor_text: And so obsequious will thy father be
summary: 'Obsequious' here does not mean servile or flattering (its modern sense) but means 'dutiful in performing funeral rites' — from Latin 'obsequiae,' funeral rites. The Father says he will faithfully perform every rite of mourning due to his son. The word is used in this older sense by Shakespeare several times; modern readers who know only the newer meaning will misread the line.

sources.name: OED

'Obsequious' in the funerary/dutiful sense (from 'obsequiae') is well-attested for Shakespeare and the Hamlet 1.2.92 parallel is a genuine supporting instance; the note that modern readers will misread it as 'servile' is accurate and useful.

anchor_text: Warwick rages like a chafed bull
summary: 'Chafed' means enraged by heat of battle or by being rubbed raw — the word comes from 'chauffer' (to heat) and in this sense means maddened by friction or excitement. A 'chafed bull' is a bull goaded into fury. The Lancastrian Prince Edward's one line of dialogue casts Warwick as a raging animal — an image consistent with Warwick's outsized, terrifying presence as 'the Kingmaker' who has turned the battle against them.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1169

'Chafed' meaning enraged/goaded (from 'chauffer') is the standard Shakespearean sense and the OED support is accurate; the characterization of Warwick as 'the Kingmaker' is historically appropriate for this point in the play.

anchor_text: Here burns my candle out; ay, here it dies
summary: Clifford's dying speech opens with a candle metaphor: his life is a candle he has burned in Henry's service, and its extinction signals Lancaster's fall. The conceit runs through the next lines — the light Clifford gave the king, the friends ('tough commixtures') who will now melt away like wax.
detail: The candle-as-life metaphor was a Christian commonplace (Proverbs 20:27, 'The spirit of man is the candle of the Lord'), but Clifford applies it to loyalty rather than soul: he has been Henry's light and warmth, and without that light the king is left in darkness. The next move — gnats flying to the sun, 'who shines now but Henry's enemies?' — pivots the light imagery from Clifford to the Yorkists, making Clifford's death a kind of solar eclipse for the Lancastrian cause. The entire monologue is structured as a dying man's valediction to his cause, a form known in the rhetoric manuals as an apostrophe (direct address to an absent party: 'O Lancaster!').

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911; rev. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'candle' (life compared to a candle, common in Shakespeare).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1183

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, is a real reference work that attests the candle-as-life metaphor in Shakespeare; the Proverbs 20:27 reference appears only in the discursive detail text, not as a cited source, so the single source cited (Onions) stands — though editors should note the Geneva 1599 reads 'light/breath,' not 'candle,' which is the KJV reading.

The candle-as-life conceit is soundly identified, the Proverbs allusion is used illustratively rather than overreached as a direct source, and the monologue structure as apostrophe is correct — the solar-eclipse extension of the light imagery through to the gnats/sun lines is well-grounded in the text itself.

anchor_text: Phoebus, hadst thou never given consent That Phaethon should check thy fiery steeds
summary: Clifford blames Henry for letting the realm spin out of control, just as the sun-god Phoebus erred in letting his son Phaethon try to drive the sun's chariot. Phaethon could not control the horses and scorched the earth until Zeus had to strike him down. The implication: Henry, like Phoebus, indulged a situation he should have mastered, and England has been 'scorch'd' as a result.
detail: Ovid's Metamorphoses (2.1-400), widely read in Golding's English translation (1567), told how Phaethon ('shining') begged his father Phoebus Apollo to let him drive the solar chariot for one day. The horses bolted; Phaethon could not 'check' (rein in) them; the earth burned until Zeus killed the boy with a thunderbolt and restored order. To 'check' the steeds means to rein them back. In the parallel, Henry is Phoebus (the king-as-sun was Elizabethan commonplace), the uncontrollable Yorkist faction is the fire-horses, and the civil-war devastation is the scorched earth. Phaethon already appeared as an image of fatal overreach in 1 Henry VI; here it is turned to condemn passivity rather than presumption.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.1-400; Arthur Golding, The .xv. Bookes of P. Ouidius Naso (1567). The same allusion appears in Richard II 3.3.178.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1193
Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.1-400 is the correct locus for the Phaethon narrative; Arthur Golding's 1567 English translation is real and widely attested; the cross-reference to Richard II 3.3 is accurate.

The Phaethon-as-Henry parallel is mainstream and defensible: Clifford explicitly invokes Phoebus's consent and Phaethon's inability to 'check' the steeds, and the mapping of Henry as the permissive sun-king whose indulgence caused devastation is what the text supports; the note rightly distinguishes this inversion (passivity, not presumption) from earlier Phaethon uses.

anchor_text: what doth cherish weeds but gentle air? And what makes robbers bold but too much lenity
summary: Clifford ends his speech with two parallel rhetorical questions: gentle air nurtures weeds; too much leniency emboldens thieves. Both assert that Henry's kindness — his defining virtue and his political failure — is what allowed the Yorkist 'weeds' to grow and the 'robbers' (the rebels) to grow bold. The figure is anaphora: the same grammatical structure repeated to drive a point home.
detail: The garden-as-kingdom metaphor was firmly established in the history plays (the allegorical garden scene in Richard II 3.4); Clifford turns it into a two-beat indictment. 'Lenity' (from Latin lenitas, mildness) is the archaic noun for gentleness or clemency. The rhetorical form is erotema (a question posed to assert, not to inquire, also called a rhetorical question): the speaker supplies the implied answer. This is also a compressed exemplum from statecraft: Elizabethan political writing (e.g. Thomas Elyot, The Boke Named the Governour, 1531) routinely warned that a prince too merciful invites disorder.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'lenity' (clemency, forbearance) and 'cherish' (encourage, foster).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1203
Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), is a real standard reference; both headwords cited ('lenity' and 'cherish') are genuine entries with the meanings claimed.

The identification of erotema (rhetorical question as assertion) and the garden-as-kingdom parallel to Richard II are both sound; the Elyot reference is used only as illustrative context for the general Elizabethan topos, not as a claimed direct source, so no overreach.

anchor_text: Bootless are plaints, and cureless are my wounds
summary: 'Bootless' means useless or without profit — from the Old English word 'bot,' meaning remedy or benefit; something bootless brings no benefit ('no boot'). 'Plaints' are laments or complaints. So: 'Lamentations are useless, and my wounds cannot be healed.' Clifford accepts that prayer and complaint are equally futile; he is a dying man trapped between the enemy and the inevitability of death.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary (1911; rev. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'bootless' (unavailing, fruitless) and 'plaint' (lamentation).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1205
Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, is real and does attest 'bootless' (unavailing, fruitless) and 'plaint' (lamentation) with those definitions.

The etymology of 'bootless' from OE 'bot' is accurate, and 'plaints' as laments is standard; the gloss correctly reads the couplet as Clifford's acceptance of futility — straightforward archaic-vocabulary annotation with no interpretive overreach.

anchor_text: as doth a sail, fill'd with a fretting gust, Command an argosy to stem the waves
summary: Edward compares Margaret to a wind-filled sail that drives a great merchant ship despite the ship having no will of its own: she propelled the passive Henry like a wind propels a vessel. An 'argosy' is a large merchant ship; a 'fretting gust' is a chafing, driving wind. The metaphor captures both Margaret's forcefulness and Henry's passivity — he was steered by her, not the other way around.
detail: The word 'argosy' probably derives from Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik), a major Adriatic trading port whose large ships were called 'raguseys' in English; by Shakespeare's time the form 'argosy' was standard for any large merchant vessel (compare The Merchant of Venice, where Antonio's argosies carry his wealth). 'Fretting' means wearing or chafing — the image of a wind straining against the sail it fills. The simile encapsulates the play's persistent characterization of Margaret as the true Lancastrian commander, with Henry as her helpless instrument — a reversal of the expected gender hierarchy of leadership.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'argosy' (a large merchant vessel, prob. from Ragusa); s.v. 'fretting' (chafing, wearing by friction).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1217
OED etymology of 'argosy' from Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik) is confirmed by multiple sources including OED itself and historical records; 'fretting' as chafing is a standard OED sense.

The argosy-from-Ragusa etymology is the mainstream scholarly account, 'fretting' as chafing is correct, and the reading of the simile as characterizing Margaret's command over the passive Henry is exactly what Edward's speech encodes; no overreach.

anchor_text: not contented that he lopp'd the branch, In hewing Rutland when his leaves put forth
summary: Richard of Gloucester charges Clifford in arboreal metaphor: Clifford was not satisfied with cutting off a branch (murdering the child Rutland) but also attacked the root — their father, the Duke of York. 'When his leaves put forth' means Rutland was just beginning to grow, a boy in the first spring of his life. The tree metaphor for dynastic lineage was conventional in heraldic and political writing, but the detail 'leaves put forth' sharpens it into grief: Clifford killed a child.
detail: The language of branches, roots, and sprays belongs to the heraldic discourse of lineage (family trees were literally drawn as trees), but Richard weaponizes it to indict Clifford for what the audience has already seen: the killing of Rutland in Act 1 and the killing of York in the same act. 'Tender spray' (line 1232) intensifies the youth of the victim — a 'spray' is a small, fresh shoot. Richard is unusual among the Yorkists here in being the most articulate about their family's grievance, a hint of his future rhetorical mastery.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-75), s.v. 'lop' (to cut branches from a tree) and 'spray' (a small shoot or branch).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1229
Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, is a real standard reference and attests 'lop' (to cut branches) and 'spray' (a small shoot or branch) with the meanings claimed.

The arboreal-lineage metaphor is correctly decoded: branch = Rutland (the child), root = York (the father), 'leaves put forth' = the boy's youth; the heraldic-family-tree context is well-attested and the claim about Richard's rhetorical precocity is textually supported without overclaiming.

anchor_text: Measure for measure must be answered
summary: Warwick declares that the Yorkists will put Clifford's head on the very gates where Clifford had placed York's head: an eye for an eye, a head for a head. 'Measure for measure' echoes the biblical principle of proportional justice — the same punishment returned in the same quantity as the original wrong.
detail: The phrase alludes to Matthew 7:2 ('with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again'; Geneva 1599) and Luke 6:38, both versions of the reciprocal-justice formula rooted in Leviticus 24:19-20 ('as he hath done, so shall it be done to him'). Shakespeare later named a whole play after this principle. In context the line is not magnanimous justice but cold lex talionis — Warwick is commanding the same public head-display that dishonored the Yorkist dead, pointing to the cycle of escalating revenge that both sides feed. Clifford's own motivation for killing Rutland and York was identical retaliation — his own father was killed at St Albans.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 7:2 (Geneva 1599): 'with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you againe.' Cf. Leviticus 24:19-20.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1237

Matthew 7:2 in the Geneva Bible 1599 reads exactly 'with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you againe,' matching the citation; Leviticus 24:19-20 is a real parallel locus for lex talionis.

The Matthew 7:2 / Luke 6:38 echo and the lex talionis framing are both defensible; the annotation correctly notes this is cold reciprocal vengeance rather than magnanimous justice, and the link to the cycle of revenge (Clifford's own rationale for killing Rutland was identical retaliation) is textually grounded and not an overreach.

anchor_text: Bring forth that fatal screech-owl to our house, That nothing sung but death to us and ours
summary: Edward calls Clifford a 'screech-owl' — a bird whose cry was a common omen of imminent death in Elizabethan popular belief. By calling him 'fatal' (death-bringing) and saying he 'sung but death,' Edward frames Clifford as a supernatural herald of doom for the house of York, recalling Clifford's murders of Rutland and York.
detail: The screech-owl (sometimes called the 'scrich-owle' or 'lich-owle') was in widespread Elizabethan folklore a harbinger of death — its cry heard at night near a house was taken as warning that someone within would soon die. Edward Hall (Union, 1548) and Holinshed record the superstition; Reginald Scot's The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) lists it among popular omens. Shakespeare uses the screech-owl as a death omen in several plays (e.g., 3 Henry VI 5.6.45, Henry VI Part 1 4.2.15). 'Ill-boding tongue' in line 1241 continues the bird omen: the owl 'speaks' doom as its song. By staging the taunts over a corpse that cannot respond, the scene also ironizes Edward's power — the 'fatal' enemy they feared is finally and utterly silent.

sources.name: Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584)
sources.citation: Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584), Book XI, ch. 16, on owls and other birds as portents of death. Cf. Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on omens before deaths.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1238

Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) is real and does catalogue popular superstitions including bird omens, but the specific chapter reference — Book XI, ch. 16 — cannot be verified and may be a fabricated locus; the general claim that Scot records owl-omen beliefs is plausible but the pinpoint citation is unconfirmed.

The screech-owl as death omen is well-attested Elizabethan folklore and the annotation reads Edward's language correctly; the only minor quibble is that the self-citation ('3 Henry VI 5.6.45') is the same play being annotated and is therefore circular, but this does not affect the interpretive verdict — the cultural context is sound.

anchor_text: Warwick cut the sea to France, And ask the Lady Bona for thy queen. So shalt thou sinew both these lands together
summary: Warwick plans to cross to France and negotiate a marriage between the new King Edward IV and Lady Bona, the sister-in-law of King Lewis XI of France. 'Sinew' here means to bind together as sinews (tendons) bind muscle to bone: the marriage would create an alliance that would neutralize the threat of French support for the exiled Lancastrians.
detail: The marriage embassy to France is Holinshed's material; it sets up the play's pivotal Act 3 scene at the French court. The dramatic irony is already in motion: the audience knows (or will learn) that Edward will impulsively marry Elizabeth Woodville (Lady Grey) before Warwick even reaches France, making the embassy a humiliation. anchor_text: For Gloster's dukedom is too ominous

An audience familiar with the preceding plays would know: Thomas of Woodstock (Duke of Gloucester, d. 1397) was smothered on Richard II's behalf, and Humphrey of Gloucester (d. 1447) was murdered in the opening of the Wars of the Roses sequence. Warwick brushes the omen aside ('Tut! that's a foolish observation'), but the audience knows that Richard — who will indeed carry the title into Richard III — is the most dangerous man in the room. anchor_text: Thy balm wash'd off wherewith thou wast anointed
summary: 'Balm' here means the consecrated oil used to anoint a king at his coronation, a ritual drawn from the Old Testament practice of anointing Israel's kings. Henry speaks of himself in the second person, numbering the signs of his deposed kingship: his throne is filled, his scepter seized, and the sacred oil rubbed away. For an Elizabethan audience anointing was not merely ceremonial — it was the act that made a king God's deputy on earth, so washing it off is near-sacrilege.
detail: The coronation anointing was based on the biblical anointing of Saul and David (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13) and carried over into Christian monarchy. The formula used in English coronations, unchanged through much of the medieval period, consecrated the king specifically through holy chrism on the hands, breast, shoulders, elbows, and head. Because the anointing was an unrepeatable sacramental act, the question of whether a deposed king could be re-anointed — and whether an un-anointed rival was truly king — was theologically explosive. Henry returns to the image at TLN 1368: he was anointed at nine months old, establishing his kingship before he could even speak.

anchor_text: No bending knee will call thee Caesar now
summary: Henry uses 'Caesar' not as a personal name but as a title meaning supreme ruler. After Julius Caesar's murder and the rise of Augustus, 'Caesar' became the standard Latin title for Roman emperors — and by extension, in medieval and early modern Europe, a byword for any sovereign of absolute power. Henry is saying no one will bow to him or call him 'my lord and king' any longer.

In Shakespeare's England the word retained its antique imperial resonance — to invoke Caesar was to invoke the pinnacle of earthly power. Henry's painful survey of what he has lost (throne, sceptre, anointing, petitioners, now the very title) ends with the most grandiose possible royal address, the more crushing because it has been reduced to nothing.

anchor_text: And Nero will be tainted with remorse
summary: Nero was the Roman emperor (reigned 54-68 CE) notorious as the supreme example of savage cruelty — among other crimes, he murdered his own mother and was blamed for burning Rome. The strategy is to persuade himself that Margaret might yet win Lewis of France over even though Warwick's suit is stronger — a self-consoling fantasy of his helplessness. Nero is also invoked at Hamlet 3.2.390-392 when Hamlet warns himself not to let 'the soul of Nero enter this firm bosom.'

anchor_text: My crown is in my heart, not on my head
summary: Henry distinguishes between the outward crown — the jeweled physical object now on Edward IV's head — and an inner kingship of conscience and contentment. This is the play's clearest statement of Henry's Stoic-Christian resignation: stripped of every external sign of rule, he locates his kingship in a place no one can seize. The keeper immediately turns the paradox against him: a crown of 'content' and a real crown are not the same when soldiers come to arrest you.

But Henry's formulation is also a kind of willed self-consolation that the play subjects to irony: the keeper's dry reply ('Your crown content and you must be contented / To go along with us') uses Henry's own word 'content' three times to spring the trap. Henry's 'crown' of contentment does him no good in the world. The scene is a miniature de casibus: the man at the bottom of Fortune's wheel trying to redefine what the top meant.

anchor_text: Look, as I blow this feather from my face
summary: Henry builds an extended simile — a feather obeying whichever wind blows strongest — to describe the political fickleness of common men. He blows the feather away, it drifts back; another gust takes it again; always 'commanded by the greater gust.' The point is that the keepers' loyalty shifts with whichever king has more force behind him, not with any principled allegiance. The image is also quietly self-aware: Henry himself is the feather, tossed about by powers far larger than he is.
detail: The device is a formal simile introduced by 'Look, as... Such is': the rhetorical term is a similitude or extended comparison. Its effect here is double-edged. Henry means to rebuke the keepers for their inconstancy, but the feather he holds in his own hand — which drifts back when he blows it, only to be blown away again — maps perfectly onto Henry's own career: he has twice been king, twice lost the throne, and now drifts back across the border like a feather on the wind. The audience is invited to see what Henry does not quite see about himself. The same image of a passive, wind-driven lightness contrasts sharply with the active, willed force of Richard, Edward, and Warwick elsewhere in the play.

anchor_text: In God's name lead; your king's name be obey'd
summary: Henry accepts arrest by separating 'God's name' from 'your king's name' — implying that Edward IV is the keepers' temporal king but that God's authority stands apart and above him. He then adds a third submission: 'what he will, I humbly yield unto' — where 'he' is deliberately ambiguous, meaning both God and Edward, collapsing the two. This quiet, passive acceptance is characteristic of Henry throughout the play and contrasts with every other character's will to power.
detail: The passage enacts the doctrine that a king rules under God and derives authority from God, so obedience to a lawful king and obedience to God ought to be the same thing. But Henry's word order keeps the two authorities distinct, with God's name coming first and given priority. His submission is not defeat in the usual sense: he is choosing to yield rather than being broken, and his three-part closing speech has a liturgical rhythm ('In God's name... your king's name... what God will... what he will') that frames arrest as an act of piety. Henry's passivity here is both his defining virtue and the quality that has cost England a civil war.

anchor_text: Would he were wasted, marrow, bones, and all, That from his loins no hopeful branch may spring

The dynastic tree metaphor ('loins' / 'branch') is conventional and the reading of this passage as Richard's first full declaration of ambition for the throne is mainstream and textually supported; Holinshed as a general citation for Yorkist succession context is appropriate.

anchor_text: stands upon a promontory, And spies a far-off shore where he would tread, Wishing his foot were equal with his eye
summary: Richard compares his desire for the crown to a man standing on a clifftop ('promontory') who can see a distant shore he wants to reach — his eye ranges farther than his feet can carry him. It is a sustained simile (a classical 'comparatio') for the gap between ambition and current power. The fantastical conclusion — that the man would 'lade it dry' (bail out the sea one bucket at a time) to get there — captures the reckless scale of Richard's determination.

The promontory/distant-shore simile is accurately identified as a sustained comparatio and 'lade it dry' (bail out the sea) is the correct gloss; the annotation does not over-read — it sticks to what the text actually says about Richard's ambition.

anchor_text: love forswore me in my mother's womb; And, for I should not deal in her soft laws, She did corrupt frail nature with some bribe To shrink mine arm up like a wither'd shrub
summary: Richard describes his physical deformities as Venus's deliberate revenge: because he was not to 'deal in' love's business (i.e., was unfit for romance and sexual life), Love bribed Nature in the womb to cripple him — a withered arm, a hump on his back, unequal legs, a general disproportion. Shakespeare builds on the Tudor chronicle tradition that Richard of Gloucester was deformed; here Richard himself turns the deformity into a dramatic origin story that explains and justifies his murderous ambition.
detail: The historical Richard III had scoliosis (confirmed by the 2012 discovery of his skeleton in Leicester), which would have caused some degree of spinal curvature, but Tudor chroniclers — especially Thomas More — greatly exaggerated it into a symbolic monstrousness. Shakespeare inherits and dramatizes that tradition. The 'unlick'd bear-whelp' image (1565-66) alludes to the Elizabethan belief that a mother bear licks her formless newborn into proper shape: Richard compares himself to a cub whose dam never completed the task. The passage is the seed of the great opening speech of Richard III ('I, that am curtail'd of this fair proportion').

sources.name: More, History of King Richard III (c. 1513-18)

The Tudor chronicle tradition of Richard's deformity and the More-Hall-Holinshed transmission line are accurately described; the note about the 2012 skeleton find and scoliosis is a factual aside that correctly contextualizes without over-claiming Shakespeare's intent.

anchor_text: like to a chaos, or an unlick'd bear-whelp That carries no impression like the dam
summary: An 'unlick'd bear-whelp' refers to a popular belief that bear cubs were born as formless lumps of flesh and that their mother's licking literally shaped them into proper bears. Richard calls himself such a whelp — unfinished, shapeless, carrying no resemblance to its parent ('no impression like the dam'). The image extends to 'chaos': both mean a mass before order or proper form has been imposed on it.

The bear-licking belief is well-attested in Pliny and its Renaissance reception, and the 'chaos' / unformed-mass parallel is accurate; the annotation does not over-extend the image.

anchor_text: I'll drown more sailors than the mermaid shall, I'll slay more gazers than the basilisk
summary: Richard lists two mythological killers he will surpass. Mermaids (or Sirens) lured sailors to their deaths with song. The basilisk was a legendary serpent or reptile whose mere gaze was lethal — it killed by looking at you. Richard claims he will outdo both: he will use charm and deceit to destroy more people than either creature ever did.
detail: Both figures are commonplaces of Elizabethan bestiary lore. The basilisk (also called the cockatrice) was described by Pliny and repeated by all the standard natural-history writers as a creature whose breath and sight caused death. The mermaid conflates the Siren of Homer's Odyssey with medieval mermaid traditions. Richard is assembling a catalogue of seductive and deadly creatures that he can beat — the speech is competitive, comic, and terrifying at once.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 8.33 (on the basilisk and its lethal gaze); Homer, Odyssey 12.39-54 (the Sirens); cf. OED s.v. 'basilisk' n., sense 1.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1590
Pliny 8.33 on the basilisk's lethal gaze is confirmed; Homer Odyssey 12.39-54 is Circe's description of the Sirens to Odysseus — the canonical locus — and accurately supports the mermaid/Siren claim.

The basilisk gloss is sound, but the annotation conflates mermaids with Sirens — they are distinct in classical and Elizabethan lore (Sirens lure with song; mermaids are associated with drowning but not primarily with song-based enticement in Tudor bestiary traditions), and the equation may be an oversimplification that a skeptical editor would flag.

anchor_text: I'll play the orator as well as Nestor, Deceive more slyly than Ulysses could, And like a Sinon take another Troy
summary: Richard invokes three figures from the Trojan War. Nestor was the oldest and most eloquent Greek counsellor — a byword for persuasive oratory. Ulysses (Odysseus) was the cleverest and most deceptive of the Greeks. Sinon was the Greek spy who talked the Trojans into dragging the wooden horse inside their walls, thereby destroying Troy from within. Richard claims he will outdo all three — speak, deceive, and hollow out a kingdom as Sinon did Troy.
detail: The three names form an ascending scale of treachery: Nestor's wisdom (oratory), Ulysses' cunning (strategy), and Sinon's outright fraud (a lie that destroys a civilization). Shakespeare knew all three from Virgil's Aeneid — Sinon's speech is recounted in Book 2 — and from Ovid's Metamorphoses 13. The Trojan War frame also recurs in the play's imagery: Warwick refers to himself and others using Trojan comparisons. Richard caps the whole list with Proteus and Machiavel, completing a bravura catalogue of shape-shifting and deceit.

sources.name: Virgil, Aeneid

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1592

Virgil Aeneid 2.57-194 covers Sinon's deception (the annotation says 2.57-198, a 4-line overshoot but not a fabrication); Iliad 1.247-252 for Nestor's honey-tongued oratory is confirmed; Ovid Metamorphoses 13 covers the Ulysses/Ajax debate showing Ulysses' cunning — all citations real and supportive.

Nestor as eloquent elder counsellor, Ulysses as the cunning deceiver, and Sinon as the spy who talked the Trojans into accepting the wooden horse are all accurate identifications; the ascending-scale-of-treachery reading is mainstream and Virgil Aeneid 2 is the correct Sinon source.

anchor_text: I can add colours to the chameleon, Change shapes with Protheus for advantages
summary: The chameleon was famous for changing its skin colour to blend with its surroundings — a Renaissance emblem of the flatterer and dissembler. Proteus (or Protheus) was the shape-shifting sea-god of Greek myth who could change into any form to escape being held. Richard claims he can out-chameleon the chameleon and out-Proteus Proteus: his disguise and adaptability will exceed anything nature or myth has produced.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1595

The chameleon-as-flatterer emblem and Proteus as shape-shifter are correct Renaissance commonplaces; the claim that Richard boasts he can exceed both is an accurate reading of 'I can add colours to the chameleon / Change shapes with Protheus for advantages.'

anchor_text: set the murtherous Machiavel to school
summary: 'Machiavel' refers to the Italian writer Niccolo Machiavelli, whose book The Prince was read in England as a handbook for amoral statecraft — using deceit, cruelty, and hypocrisy to seize and hold power. To 'set him to school' means to teach even Machiavelli a lesson, to outdo the master of villainy. Richard is boasting that his ruthlessness and cunning surpass the worst tyrant the imagination can supply.
detail: Few Elizabethans read Machiavelli directly; the popular bogeyman came mainly through Innocent Gentillet's hostile Contre-Machiavel (1576) and through the theatre, where 'Machiavel' became shorthand for atheistic, murderous scheming. Richard III is the supreme English example of the type. The soliloquy effectively writes the character of the Richard III play that is coming: a theatrical villain who confides his plots to the audience with gleeful relish.

sources.name: Machiavelli, The Prince (1532)
sources.citation: Niccolo Machiavelli, Il Principe (written 1513, printed 1532); Innocent Gentillet, Contre-Machiavel (1576, English 1602), the popular hostile digest that gave Elizabethans their 'Machiavel' caricature.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1597
Il Principe was written 1513 and printed 1532 (correct); Gentillet's Contre-Machiavel appeared in French in 1576 and in Simon Patericke's English translation in 1602 (both dates confirmed).

The 'Machiavel' as Elizabethan stage bogeyman rather than careful reader of Il Principe is the standard scholarly position, and the Gentillet-as-intermediary note is accurate; 'set him to school' meaning to outdo the master is correct.

anchor_text: Must strike her sail and learn a while to serve
summary: 'Strike sail' means to lower a ship's sail as a sign of surrender or submission. Margaret is using a nautical metaphor: she, once a queen who commanded, must now make herself humble before a foreign king who can help her. Sailors struck sail to show deference when passing a warship or entering port.
detail: The image of lowering sails to yield precedence was conventional for political submission; it recurs across Shakespeare's histories (Richard II uses it of subjects bowing before kings). Here it also prepares the audience for the whole scene's reversal of Margaret's status: the sovereign who once gave orders must now beg.

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1604
OED s.v. 'strike' does carry the sense of lowering a sail in submission; the sense number may vary across OED editions but the core lexicographic claim is accurate and well-established.

The nautical submission metaphor is well-documented and the gloss accurately reads Margaret's self-humbling posture in context (TLN 1603-1610); the parallel to Richard II is a legitimate supporting parallel, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Great Albion's queen in former golden days
summary: 'Albion' is a poetic and archaic name for England, from the Latin 'Albion' used by Greek and Roman writers, perhaps from the white (Latin 'albus') chalk cliffs of the coast. Margaret calls herself queen of the whole island in its lost days of glory. The phrase 'golden days' echoes the classical idea of a Golden Age of peace and prosperity now past.
detail: Classical writers including Pliny the Elder (Natural History 4.30) used 'Albion' for Britain. Shakespeare uses it repeatedly as an elevated or nostalgic register for England (Henry V 3.5, King Lear 3.2). The 'golden days' phrase links Margaret's lost queenship to the de casibus topos — she has fallen from Fortune's wheel.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 4.30 ('Albionum insularum').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1606

'Albion' as a poetic/archaic name for England is uncontroversial, and linking 'golden days' to a lost Golden Age and the de casibus topos is mainstream-defensible given Margaret's explicit fall-from-Fortune framing in the same speech.

anchor_text: yield not thy neck / To fortune's yoke, but let thy dauntless mind / Still ride in triumph over all mischance
summary: Lewis tells Margaret not to bow to 'Fortune's yoke' — the yoke being the wooden collar used to harness oxen, here a metaphor for being enslaved by bad luck. Fortune (Latin Fortuna) was imagined as a goddess who turned a great wheel, raising and crushing kings and heroes at random. Lewis urges Margaret to let her spirit triumph over the turning wheel rather than submit to it.
detail: The image of Fortune's yoke is an inversion of the Boethian consolation: Boethius's Philosophy (Consolatio II) teaches the prisoner to resist Fortune by knowing her nature. Lewis here applies the counter-advice — resist her, don't yield. The military metaphor 'ride in triumph' also echoes the Roman triumph, the victory procession, and contrasts with the 'struck sail' of 1604.

sources.name: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 (Fortune's wheel and the wise man's response).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1616

Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae Book II, prose 1-2, is the canonical locus for Fortune's wheel and the philosopher's response; the source is real and supports the gloss, even though the annotation slightly mischaracterises the direction of Boethius's advice (acceptance rather than defiant resistance).

Fortune-as-yoke and the Boethian consolation framework are standard readings; Lewis's counter-counsel ('ride in triumph') is a legitimate inversion of Boethian acceptance, not an overreach, and the Roman triumph echo is supported by TLN 1618's phrasing.

anchor_text: proud ambitious Edward, Duke of York, / Usurps the regal title and the seat / Of England's true-anointed lawful king
summary: Margaret summarizes the Yorkist takeover. Edward (York's eldest son) has proclaimed himself King Edward IV and driven Henry VI — the Lancastrian king crowned and 'anointed' at his coronation — into exile in Scotland. 'True-anointed' stresses that Henry was consecrated with holy oil at his coronation, making his kingship divinely sealed; to remove him is therefore sacrilege, not just politics.
detail: This is Margaret's partisan framing of events Shakespeare staged in Acts 1-2. 'Anointed' carries the weight of divine-right ideology: consecration with chrism oil was the ceremony that, in Elizabethan thinking, transferred God's authority to a monarch; hence 'usurp' implies not merely seizing a throne but violating sacred order. Holinshed records Henry's flight to Scotland after Towton (1461) and Edward's proclamation as king. The tension between Margaret's 'true-anointed' and Warwick's counter-claim that Henry 'usurp'd' (TLN 1682) is the scene's ideological axis.

sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), Vol. III, under Henry VI and Edward IV, on the flight to Scotland after Towton.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1628
Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) Vol. III does record Henry VI's flight to Scotland after Towton (1461) and Edward's proclamation as king; the historical claims are accurate and well-sourced.
The annotation accurately glosses 'true-anointed' using divine-right ideology and correctly frames this as Margaret's partisan perspective; the reading is mainstream and grounded in the text.

anchor_text: now begins a second storm to rise, / For this is he that moves both wind and tide
summary: Margaret compares Warwick's entry to a second storm blowing into the court, and calls him 'he that moves both wind and tide' — a man with the power of nature itself, able to shift the winds of politics and the tides of war in any direction. The phrase is a metaphor for Warwick's reputation as 'the Kingmaker': the mightiest subject in England, who has already toppled one king (Henry) and can topple another.
detail: The storm imagery returns from TLN 1639, where Lewis told Margaret to 'calm the storm.' Warwick 'moves both wind and tide' extends the metaphor into hyperbole: a man who controls both the atmosphere and the sea is a force beyond human scale. The compliment is backhanded — omnipotence of this kind in a subject is dangerous. Holinshed calls Warwick 'chief doer and worker' in Edward's rise (Chronicles, 1587, Vol. III).

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), Vol. III: characterization of the Earl of Warwick.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1648
Holinshed does characterise Warwick as the driving force behind Edward IV's rise; the rhetorical-device analysis requires no external source beyond the primary text.

The storm metaphor is explicit in the text (TLN 1639 and 1648) and the reading of 'moves both wind and tide' as hyperbole for Warwick's Kingmaker power is defensible; calling the compliment 'backhanded' is a reasonable dramatic inference, not speculation.

anchor_text: to crave a league of amity; / And lastly, to confirm that amity / With nuptial knot
summary: Warwick has come to France on three linked missions: to greet Lewis, to propose a formal alliance ('league of amity') between England and France, and to seal that alliance with a royal marriage. The proposed bride is Lady Bona, Lewis's sister-in-law. In the diplomacy of the period, peace treaties were routinely 'confirmed' by arranged royal marriages to tie the two dynasties together and make war between them a family matter.
detail: Historically, Edward IV did send Warwick to France in 1464 to negotiate a French alliance and a marriage to the French princess. The mission was undercut when Edward secretly married Elizabeth Woodville (Lady Grey) in May 1464 — news that arrived while Warwick was still in France. Holinshed records Warwick's fury and humiliation (Chronicles, 1587, Vol. III). Shakespeare compresses the timeline slightly but follows the broad shape of events, and the insult to Warwick's personal honour (pledging the king's love while the king was already married in secret) is the hinge on which the scene and the whole Yorkist alliance turns.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), Vol. III: Warwick's embassy to France and the Lady Bona negotiations, 1464.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1654
Holinshed (1587) Vol. III records Warwick's 1464 embassy to France, the Lady Bona negotiation, and Edward's secret marriage to Elizabeth Woodville; the historical claims are accurate.

The historical account of Warwick's 1464 French embassy and the Bona negotiation is accurate and the dramatic summary of how Edward's secret Woodville marriage undercut it is well-established by Holinshed and the scene's own plot.

anchor_text: Where fame, late entering at his heedful ears, / Hath plac'd thy beauty's image and thy virtue
summary: Warwick personifies 'fame' as a messenger who slipped into Edward's ear and implanted an image of Bona's beauty there. 'Fame' here is the classical figure Fama (Rumour), the winged goddess of report who carries news across the world. Ovid describes Fama as dwelling in a house between heaven, earth, and sea, with a thousand windows through which every whisper passes (Metamorphoses 12.39-63).
detail: Warwick's courtly praise borrows the language of Petrarchan love-poetry (beauty's 'image' seated in the lover's soul) but also frames it as natural report rather than personal passion, which suits an ambassador-in-love making a proxy suit. The irony is sharp: fame has just betrayed Edward by reporting his secret marriage to Lady Grey, which the Post will deliver at TLN 1780.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 12.39-63 (Golding trans. 1567, Book XII), describing the house of Fama/Fame/Rumour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1665

Ovid, Metamorphoses 12.39-63 (confirmed via the Virginia Ovid text) is precisely the House of Fama/Rumour passage with a thousand windows; the line range and Golding translation (1567, Book XII) are correct.

The primary sense here is simply 'rumour/report' entered through the ear — a routine Elizabethan topos — and invoking Ovid's Fama palace (Met. 12) specifically is plausible but not compelled by the text; the annotation should not be refuted but the Ovidian allusion is not certain rather than merely incidental.

anchor_text: how can tyrants safely govern home / Unless abroad they purchase great alliance
summary: Margaret argues that Edward's desire for a French alliance proves he is a tyrant insecure at home: a legitimate king does not need to 'purchase' foreign friends to prop up his rule. 'Purchase' here means to obtain or acquire (not necessarily by paying money). The argument is that only usurpers and tyrants need diplomatic marriages as political insurance against domestic rivals.
detail: The logic is a standard piece of anti-tyranny rhetoric: legitimate authority is self-sustaining, while illegitimate power must constantly buy support. It anticipates the Machiavellian critique that Edward is acting from calculated 'necessity' (TLN 1670) rather than honest affection — which, as the scene quickly reveals, is exactly true, since he has already secretly married elsewhere. The argument works doubly as self-contradiction: Henry VI also needs foreign alliance, which is why Margaret is here.
